item.title: Mob attacks on political party offices raise questions about police role
item.description:
Former Bangladesh Chhatra union president Dipak Shil was detained on Monday while attempting to join a human chain in Dhaka’s Dhanmondi to protest the obstruction of female Baul singers in Sunamganj from performing. After his release, CPB leaders and activists brought out a procession on Monday night. The procession ended at Paltan intersection, where participants held a brief rally and chanted “Joy Bangla, Joy Samajtantra (Socialism)”.

Following this, 40 to 50 people identifying themselves as leaders and activists of Jubo Dal and Chhatra Dal protested against the “Joy Bangla” slogan. An exchange of words between the two groups escalated, and two CPB leaders and activists were beaten. The attackers subsequently gathered outside the CPB’s central office with sticks and clubs, chanting various slogans. The situation eventually calmed down without escalating into a major confrontation.

In a statement issued after the incident, CPB president Kazi Sajjad Zahir Chandan and general secretary Abdullah Kafi Ratan said a group of people carrying sticks and clubs, identifying themselves as supporters of the ruling party, had gathered in front of Mukti Bhaban in Purana Paltan. Claiming that members of the banned Awami League were inside the CPB’s central office, they attempted to break through the main gate. When CPB leaders and activists resisted, the group attacked them, leaving several people injured.

The statement further said that even after police arrived and took responsibility for securing the office, the attackers continued to blockade it for an extended period. They kept demanding that the alleged members of the banned party inside the office be handed over to them. CPB leaders described the incident as a direct assault on free political activity and peaceful coexistence, demanding that the attackers be identified and brought to justice.

Repeated incidents of mobs surrounding political party offices, leaders’ homes and political programmes cannot be dismissed as trivial. The implications for law enforcement are particularly serious when members of the ruling party and its affiliated organisations are found to be involved.
A female Baul singer performs at a musical gathering in the courtyard of expatriate Shawkat Ali’s house in Hatia village, Dirai upazila, Sunamganj, on Thursday night.

Recently, leaders and activists of the BNP and its affiliated organisations, including Jubo Dal, surrounded the JSD office in Gulistan, Dhaka, and exerted pressure on the party. Subsequently, instead of taking action against BNP activists, law enforcement agencies arrested JSD leaders and activists. Earlier, during the interim government’s tenure, the Jatiya Party’s offices were attacked and set on fire several times. More recently, a procession attacked the residence of Jatiya Party chairman GM Quader in Uttara.

Following the July mass uprising, the Awami League government fell on 5 August 2024. For several days afterwards, the country effectively had no functioning government. In the resulting vacuum of state authority, political party offices in various parts of the country were attacked, vandalised and set on fire. Some attacks targeted Awami League offices, while others affected different institutions. Political anger, revenge and long-standing grievances may have contributed to these incidents.

At the time, many viewed the attacks as expressions of immediate anger. Some hoped they would stop once the situation returned to normal. Yet, two years later, political party offices and leaders’ homes are still being attacked. It is increasingly difficult to dismiss these incidents merely as a consequence of the post-uprising situation. Instead, they raise questions about political tolerance, the government’s responsibilities and the capacity of law enforcement agencies.

The recent incidents differ in their political contexts and patterns. However, they share one common feature: in almost every case, activists of the ruling party have been at the forefront, while law enforcement agencies have taken positions against the victims, effectively acting on behalf of those activists.

The BNP came to power in February with a two-thirds majority. The party is generally regarded as centrist. Its leaders have also spoken in favour of political tolerance in their speeches and statements, advocating a new kind of politics that moves beyond extremism and the suppression of dissent. The path the country takes now depends on the choices made by the BNP, the government and law enforcement agencies.

Why is the CPB being targeted?

During the ousted Awami League government’s tenure, opposition parties boycotted the 2014 and 2024 elections. The CPB also stayed away from both polls. The party consistently spoke out against the Awami League’s repression and anti-people activities. During the July mass uprising, the CPB and its former leaders openly sided with the students and the public. Yet the party is now being treated as an adversary. It remains to be seen whether policymakers in the ruling BNP will tolerate this or rein in their party’s activists.

The CPB has alleged that following Monday night’s attack, police detained two of its members, Iran Molla and Sohel Fakir. Both were released late at night.

Anyone who objects to a political slogan has the right to protest against it. But such objections cannot justify assaulting members of another party or threatening them outside their offices. Nor is it the responsibility of party activists to determine whether a political slogan violates the law.

Earlier, cultural activists had called a human chain in Dhanmondi on Monday afternoon to protest the obstruction of female Baul singers in Sunamganj. They gathered in front of Meena Bazar at Dhanmondi 27, but police prevented them from holding the protest. Former Chhatra Union president Dipak Shil was detained from the scene and released at around 9pm. There have also been allegations that ruling party activists were present alongside police. This raises serious questions about the role of law enforcement agencies.

Over the past year, Baul singers have been attacked in Manikganj, Sherpur and Sylhet. Protests against these incidents have also been obstructed and attacked. This naturally raises a question for any concerned citizen: does this mean that protests are now prohibited in the country? The July mass uprising stands as one of the most powerful demonstrations of protest by the country’s students and citizens. Why, then, should people be prevented from protesting now?

27 arrested from JASAD office

On 26 September, police detained 289 people during a central council meeting of JSD at the party’s central office in Gulistan, Dhaka. Of them, 27 were subsequently shown as arrested. They were accused of chanting “Joy Bangla” inside the office to intimidate others and create an unstable situation.

JSD said it had organised the meeting with permission from the Dhaka Metropolitan Police. Around 400 leaders and activists from different parts of the country attended. The party alleged that BNP activists attacked its office while the meeting was underway. Police subsequently arrived, cordoned off the office and detained those present. They even locked the party office, although law enforcement agencies later handed JSD leaders the keys to unlock it.

Almost all 27 people who were arrested have since secured bail. During the operation, law enforcement personnel had claimed that members of the Awami League, whose activities are banned, had gathered at the JSD office. However, they ultimately failed to substantiate that claim. Questions have therefore arisen over whether the allegations against the detainees were fabricated.

JSD was an ally of the ousted Awami League government. However, the party itself is not banned under the country’s laws. Police may take action if a crime is committed during a political party meeting, but any such action must be based on specific allegations and evidence. Detaining everyone simply because they were present at an office, and subsequently arresting some of them, must be regarded as excessive.

Jatiya Party repeatedly targeted

The Jatiya Party and its late chairman, HM Ershad, are often described as among the most opportunistic political party and leader in Bangladesh’s political history. When opposition parties, including the BNP, boycotted the 2014 election, Ershad, his party and its leaders participated in the one-sided polls and fully enjoyed their share of power. They simultaneously served in the government and in the opposition, earning the reputation of a “domesticated opposition” in the country.

The party has paid a price for that role. It split several times while Ershad was alive and fragmented further after 5 August 2024. Its public support has dwindled to a historic low. For the first time, none of its candidates won a seat in the most recent election. In most constituencies, the party could not even mount a meaningful contest. Yet, at one time, it was considered the country’s third political force.

In other words, the people have already passed their judgment on the Jatiya Party’s past role. Even so, its offices and leaders continue to be targeted. During the interim government’s tenure, the party’s offices were attacked and set on fire on several occasions. These incidents demonstrated that the tendency to target political parties because of their identity or political positions had not disappeared. The recent attack on GM Quader’s residence in Uttara has heightened those concerns.

The BNP is now in power. The responsibility for ending political violence and ensuring the security of all parties therefore rests with the current government. If anyone uses their affiliation with the ruling party to attack another party’s office, the government cannot evade responsibility. If overzealous members of the ruling party are behind such incidents, its policymakers should rein them in.

Attacks on political party offices are not merely a problem for the parties directly affected. They have implications for the entire political environment. If a party believes that opposing the ruling party could lead to its office being attacked or its leaders and activists being harassed, conducting political activities will become increasingly difficult.

Who is exploiting political rivalries?

After Sheikh Hasina fled to India, almost all Awami League leaders went into hiding. Their party offices, homes and business establishments were left unprotected. Widespread attacks, vandalism and arson followed.

The historic residence of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman at Dhanmondi 32 was also attacked. On the night of 5 February 2025, protesters entered the house and extensively vandalised it and set it on fire following the announcement that Sheikh Hasina would deliver an online address. Much of the building was subsequently demolished using cranes and excavators. The demolition continued the following day. On 17 November of the same year, the army and police intervened when an attempt was made to demolish the remaining part of the house.

Both incidents occurred during the interim government’s tenure. There has been criticism that some online activists instigated the attacks. However, the government of the time took no action against anyone over the incidents.

Political parties will inevitably face criticism and opposition over their past conduct. Anyone accused of a crime can also be prosecuted under the existing law. But allegations of wrongdoing or political differences cannot be used to justify attacks on party offices, obstruction of meetings and rallies, or harassment of party leaders and activists.

One of the key expectations for political change following the mass uprising was freedom of expression and the right to hold dissenting opinions. That freedom must be guaranteed not just to the ruling party and its allies, but to every lawful political party. The BNP is now in government. It is therefore the government’s responsibility to act on allegations against BNP leaders and activists and ensure that law enforcement agencies remain impartial.

The recent incidents involving the CPB, JSD and the Jatiya Party are therefore not merely questions of security for a few political parties. They are also a test of how well the political system that emerged after the mass uprising protects the right to hold and express dissenting views.

item.title: HSC 2026: How to check the results
item.description:
The results of this year’s Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations will be published on 31 October.

The process of releasing the results will be formally launched at an event at the International Mother Language Institute in Segunbagicha, Dhaka, at 11:00 am that day.

As soon as the launch takes place, the results will be published simultaneously online and through the respective educational institutions.

A press release from the Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee said all respective educational institutions would have to collect the results published by the boards through the websites: https://eduboardresults.gov.bd and https://educationboardresults.gov.bd.

HSC results to be published on 31 October as date changed

The boards have advised institutions to download and publish the results online by clicking on the Results section of either website and retrieving the results using the board name and the institution’s EIIN (Educational Institution Identification Number).

Candidates will be able to access their results through the common website of the education boards and the website of their respective education board. They will also be able to collect their results from their own educational institutions.

Candidates can also obtain their results by sending an SMS to 16140 from any mobile phone number. To receive results by SMS, they must type HSC <Space>, first three letters of the board’s name <Space> roll number <Space> examination year, and send the message to 16140.

For example, they must type HSC Dha 123456 2026 and send it to 16140. Results will not be available from the Ministry of Education, education boards or newspaper offices.

When to apply for re-scrutiny

The press release said applications for re-evaluation with re-scrutiny of answer scripts would be accepted online from 1 to 7 November. The application process and relevant instructions will be published on the education boards’ websites.

Change in result publication date

According to the earlier announcement, the results of this year’s Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations were scheduled to be published on 29 October. The date has now been changed. Under the revised schedule, the results will be published on 31 October, Saturday.

SSC, HSC: Education boards ready to hold re-exams in failed subjects within 3 months

Professor Syed Akhtaruzzaman, president of the Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee and chairman of the Dhaka Education Board, informed Prothom Alo of the new date today, Tuesday, 27 October.

This year’s HSC and equivalent examinations began on 2 July. The written examinations were scheduled to end on 8 August, but several examinations under the Chattogram Education Board were postponed because of natural disasters. The postponed examinations were held later.

A total of 1,270,583 candidates, including regular and irregular examinees, sat the HSC and equivalent examinations this year. However, a considerable number of candidates were absent.

item.title: Kane says Ballon d'Or win 'feels like a dream' as tributes pour in
item.description:
SOCCER-BALLON/

Harry Kane said Tuesday that his Ballon d''Or triumph "feels like a dream" as tributes poured in for the first English winner of the award in a generation.

The England and Bayern Munich forward fended off competition from Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe to be named the world's best men's footballer at the London Palladium theatre late on Monday.

Wembley was lit up to recognise Kane's achievement, with England's X account carrying the message: "The home of the world's best footballer."

The former Tottenham forward is the first Englishman to win the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001.

The 33-year-old struck a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country last season, propelling the German giants to a league and cup double.

The England captain, who also picked up the men's striker of the year award, scored six times as his side finished third at the World Cup in North America.

"It sounds crazy to be honest but it sounds pretty good," Kane told Sky Sports on Tuesday. "What a special night. An incredible feeling. I'm still just trying to take it all in really. It feels really, really like a dream.

"The emotion (when his name was called) was relief, joy, happiness, excitement. There was so much waiting to find out the winner and in that moment it was quite nerve-wracking so to have that kind of release and to be able to share it with everyone there in that theatre was special."

Prince William, patron of the Football Association, praised the England skipper.

"What a fantastic achievement and so deserved," he wrote on Instagram.

"A brilliant captain, a remarkable player and someone who has given football fans across the world so many unforgettable moments."

Superlatives

England boss Thomas Tuchel, who was Bayern boss when Kane arrived in Germany in 2023, said the Three Lions were "lucky" to have him as their leader.

"I ran out of superlatives to describe your performances a long time ago, but I''m delighted to see that you have now been formally recognised by the football world," he said.

"To become the first Englishman to win this huge honour in 25 years makes it extra special and we are lucky to have you as our leader."

England and Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice described Kane as "incredible" while Chelsea's Morgan Rogers, another international teammate, said he was the "best ever".

Bayern Munich president Herbert Hainer said the award was "a proud day for FC Bayern".

"Harry Kane can do it all -- and he scores goals, goals and more goals. He now joins a line with Franz Beckenbauer, Gerd Muller and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge (as previous Ballon d'Or winners) -- that says everything about our history," he said.

"The club and Harry Kane have got together, grown together and achieved the highest aims together. We are proud that this all-round outstanding sportsman and person is part of our FC Bayern family."

Harry Redknapp, former Tottenham manager, described his all-round game as "brilliant".

"It isn't just his goalscoring that is good, it is his all-round play, and the way he is and the way he is around the players. He is great as the England captain," he told the BBC.

"No one could have deserved this more, it has been a brilliant story."

85 penalised without drug testing, raising widespread concerns
item.description:
An instrumental musician is one of the 85 people sentenced to imprisonment following a raid on a rented residence belonging to an Additional DIG (Deputy Inspector General) of Police. His father is a renowned member of a well-known musical band.

Speaking to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, the father claimed that his son had gone to the rented property of the Additional DIG as he was appointed to perform at the event. A mobile court sentenced him to one month’s imprisonment on charges of drug consumption. Crucially, however, no medical test was conducted to verify whether his son had actually consumed drugs.

The raid was carried out on the night of 19 October at a three-storey house named ‘Golden Sunrise’, situated in the Police Officers’ Housing Society-1 residential area at Bhatara in the capital.

Among the 85 individuals detained during the operation, 26 were women. The women were sentenced to 15 days’ imprisonment along with a fine of Tk 500 each. The men were sentenced to one month’s imprisonment and fined Tk 1,000 each.

The operation has raised serious questions:

First: Why were sentences handed down without mandatory drug testing?

Second: How was video footage recorded by the police, showing everyone crammed into two rooms, leaked and circulated publicly?

Third: Given that the plots surrounding the Additional DIG’s house are vacant, how was public peace disrupted?

Fourth: Why did the Detective Branch (DB) dismantle the building’s CCTV cameras prior to the raid, where are the memory cards containing the CCTV footage now, and why are they absent from the official seizure list?

Fifth: Police alleged that DJ parties were routinely hosted at the property, so why is DJ equipment entirely missing from the seizure list?

The raid was carried out on the night of 19 October at a three-storey house named ‘Golden Sunrise’, situated in the Police Officers’ Housing Society-1 residential area at Bhatara in the capital.

The owner of the house is Additional DIG of Police Abdullah Al Zahir, who had rented out the property. Following the raid and subsequent media coverage, Abdullah Al Zahir was relieved of his operational duties and attached to Police Headquarters.

Various civil society organisations have issued statements expressing deep concern over the incident, accompanied by growing demands for an independent investigation.

What was observed at the scene

The Police Officers’ Housing Society is an official residential project designated for police personnel. Located approximately 4.5 kilometres along the July 36 Expressway (popularly known as 300-Feet Road) from Kuril in Dhaka, the housing society lies on the left side of the avenue.

Spanning 143 acres, the project comprises roughly 1,100 plots allocated to police officers. However, the majority of the plots remain vacant, with only a few buildings constructed to date.

Additional DIG Abdullah Al Zahir’s three-storey building stands on a 3.5-katha plot. The tree-lined property features an open space of roughly two kathas at the front, which serves as the primary venue for hosting events.

Additional DIG Abdullah Al Zahir told Prothom Alo that his residence was rented out for private functions. The property is listed on Airbnb, the US-based home-sharing platform, as well as on Travela, a similar domestic platform. Furthermore, the house was let out for events through a Facebook group.

On visiting the house on Monday afternoon, the main gate was found locked. Two cars parked in front of the gate were covered in dust. According to sources, the vehicles belong to two individuals detained during the raid; no one had come to retrieve them since they were sent to prison.

What transpired on the night of the raid

The raid on the Additional DIG’s rented house was conducted by a team from the Uttara Division of the Detective Branch (DB) of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP).

Based on accounts from DMP and DB sources, relatives of the convicts, and witnesses present during the operation, guests began arriving at the residence from 8:00 pm onwards. By midnight, a total of 85 individuals had gathered in phases.

At around 12:30 am, a DB contingent of 40 to 50 officials entered the premises while the main gate was open. Upon entering, officers instructed guests socialising outside to move indoors. Subsequently, everyone was forcibly confined inside two rooms—a process that took nearly half an hour.

Sources report that police officers then searched for the CCTV cameras installed on the premises. Out of six cameras, four were dismantled and taken away. The remaining two were disconnected, and their memory cards were removed.

Following the removal of the CCTV cameras, a thorough search of the premises was conducted. Sources indicate that no narcotics were recovered during the initial search. Police officers then requested those present to hand over any illicit substances in their possession, but no one surrendered anything. A second search yielded two empty liquor bottles.

Elias Kabir, Deputy Commissioner of DB Uttara Division, DMPWe had no prior intelligence regarding the party at the residence. The raid was executed following instructions from higher police authorities.

After being detained in two rooms throughout the night, all 85 individuals were transported to the DB headquarters in the early hours of the morning, where summary sentences were handed down.

Prior to this, police officers filmed the detainees inside the rooms and recorded footage as they were being led out.

Under standard legal procedure, law enforcement agencies must prepare an official seizure list following any operation. According to the list compiled by the DB, four liquor bottles were recovered from the house: one empty 750ml bottle of locally produced Carew & Co. liquor; one 1-litre bottle of foreign liquor containing approximately 500ml; another foreign liquor bottle containing around 200ml; and a fully sealed 1-litre bottle.

The DB seizure list also recorded the recovery of a single Yaba tablet, drug-consumption paraphernalia, and a small quantity of kush.

The operation was led by the Deputy Commissioner (DC) of DB Uttara Division, Elias Kabir. When queried by Prothom Alo, he stated that they had no prior intelligence regarding the party at the residence. The raid was executed following instructions from higher police authorities, adding that illegal drug consumption and DJ parties had allegedly been hosted there for a long time.

Notably, a video circulated online showing Elias Kabir preventing a woman from covering her face during a raid at a residential hotel in the capital’s Abdullahpur bus stand area on 12 August. In the video, addressing a crying woman, he was heard saying: “Don’t cover your face, or you will be beaten.”

DMP Additional Commissioner Shafiqul Islam, who is in charge of the DBThe concerned magistrate is in the best place to answer as to what extent the offense was proven and on what basis the sentence was passed. Adjudication is not our responsibility.

Prothom Alo published a report on that incident. Commenting on the matter at the time, former member of the National Human Rights Commission Nur Khan told Prothom Alo that if a woman commits a crime, she must be tried and sentenced by a court based on evidence; however, police arranging informal punishments prior to judicial trial is strictly illegal.

Sentencing without toxicological screening

Special Metropolitan Magistrate Asaduzzaman of DMP’s Uttara Division passed the sentences on the individuals detained from the Additional DIG’s rented house. A document detailing fine collection from 40 individuals cites Section 36(5) of the Narcotics Control Act, 2018 under the offense column.

The section stipulates that if a person consumes narcotics and, in an intoxicated state, causes a breach of public peace, engages in disorderly conduct, or drives a vehicle, they shall be punished with imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year along with a fine.

When contacted, DMP Additional Commissioner Shafiqul Islam, who is in charge of the DB, told Prothom Alo, “The concerned magistrate is in the best place to answer as to what extent the offense was proven and on what basis the sentence was passed. Adjudication is not our responsibility.”

Regarding whether any of the detainees were tested for intoxication prior to sentencing, Magistrate Asaduzzaman himself confirmed to Prothom Alo that no medical tests were conducted. He stated that the accused were sentenced after pleading guilty.

Barrister Jyotirmoy BaruaIn a mobile court, the judge, jury, and executioner become one and the same entity. In the vast majority of cases, justice is denied.

However, relatives of several convicted individuals told Prothom Alo that the claim of pleading guilty is untrue. They visited the convicts in prison to clarify the matter as they prepare to lodge appeals.

The relatives further alleged that signatures were obtained on a paper under the pretext of releasing them upon signing a bond, only for them to be subsequently convicted on charges of drug consumption.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, advocate Barrister Jyotirmoy Barua stated that a guilty plea alone does not warrant conviction in a narcotics case.

Pointing out that the DB might have coerced the accused before presenting them to the magistrate, He said, “The magistrate ought to have scrutinised the DB’s allegations critically. If intoxication was suspected, there should have been no impediment to conducting tests to establish proof, especially given the accessibility of simple testing methods today.”

“In a mobile court, the judge, jury, and executioner become one and the same entity. In the vast majority of cases, justice is denied,” Jyotirmoy Barua added.

Jyotirmoy Barua expressed strong suspicion regarding the entire operation, noting that if an offense occurs at a rented property owned by a police officer, the force would typically attempt to suppress it. Conversely, conducting a raid and publicising it raises serious questions.

Those convicted in the operation are primarily entrepreneurs, employees at multinational companies and domestic corporate entities, and students from reputable universities.

According to police sources, Abdullah Al Zahir had a dispute with an influential faction within the police force over transfers of OCs and related administrative decisions. Consequently, he was removed from that division on 1 October and posted to the Maintenance and Repair branch of Police Headquarters. Shortly thereafter, the raid on his residence was executed.

A relative of one convict remarked, “The DB recovered four liquor bottles—one full, two partially full, and one empty. Did 85 individuals become intoxicated by consuming this negligible quantity of alcohol?”

He added that people have been unjustly penalised.

How the video leaked

Article 35(5) of the Constitution of Bangladesh guarantees protection in respect of trial and punishment, stating, “No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman, or degrading punishment or treatment.”

Furthermore, Articles 2(1) and 4 of the UN Convention against Torture mandate member states to enact legislation categorising torture, cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment and punishment as criminal offences.

On 11 December 2012, the High Court issued a directive restraining law enforcement agencies from presenting arrested or suspected individuals before the media.

At the time, the High Court also issued a rule asking why instructions should not be given to keep law enforcement agencies within their legal bounds. The Home Secretary, Inspector General of Police, Director General of RAB, and the DMP Commissioner among others were asked to reply within two weeks.

Since the tenure of the previous interim government, agencies including the Police, RAB, and BGB began blurring the faces of detained or arrested individuals in press releases. In this instance, however, video footage shot by police officers leaked through official channels and spread rapidly. News outlets that published the video without blurring faces have also faced public backlash.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, senior advocate of the Supreme Court Ehsanul Huq Samaji stated that there are legal limitations regarding the publication of photos or videos of accused persons.

According to him, if such photos or videos are leaked by law enforcement agencies, serious questions arise as to their authority to do so.

It is essential to examine the extent to which these legal boundaries have been violated, he added.

Operation driven by internal rift?

From the tenure of the interim government until last September, Abdullah Al Zahir served in the Personal Management-2 division at Police Headquarters. This division oversees the transfer, posting, and promotion of Officers-in-Charge (OCs), Inspectors, Assistant Sub-Inspectors (Armed), Assistant Town Sub-Inspectors (ATSI), and Nayeks.

According to police sources, Abdullah Al Zahir had a dispute with an influential faction within the police force over transfers of OCs and related administrative decisions. Consequently, he was removed from that division on 1 October and posted to the Maintenance and Repair branch of Police Headquarters. Shortly thereafter, the raid on his residence was executed.

An attempt was made to obtain a statement from DMP Additional Commissioner Shafiqul Islam regarding these allegations; however, he terminated the phone call before the question could be put to him.

Meanwhile, Additional DIG Abdullah Al Zahir told Prothom Alo, “I have been serving in the police force for 22 years. If any allegation arose against me, a basic inquiry or verification could have been conducted.”

Demands for an independent inquiry

In response to the arrest and summary conviction of 85 individuals, including women, 101 prominent citizens issued a joint statement on Sunday expressing deep concern and protest.

They demanded the immediate release of the detainees and convicts, an independent investigation into the incident, and accountability for those who violated legal norms.

They also called for an immediate end to encroachments on citizens’ personal lives, privacy, and dignity.

In a separate statement issued on Sunday, human rights organisations including BLAST, Human Rights Support Society (HRSS), Naripokkho, and Sopran called for an end to mass sentencing via mobile courts.

The statement urged that an impartial investigation be conducted to ascertain whether there was an abuse of power or rights violation during the arrest and sentencing, and that those responsible be held accountable.

Concurrently, they demanded action against those responsible for unlawfully collecting, circulating, and publishing the personal data, images, videos, and identities of the detainees.

A relative of one of the convicts, speaking anonymously, urged, “Let there be an impartial investigation into this incident. That is our sole expectation from the government.”

item.title: MP's son questioned in police custody over Chhatra Dal leader's death
item.description:
Police have taken Nuruzzaman, the eldest son of BNP lawmaker Abdul Aziz from Natore-4 (Gurudaspur-Baraigram) constituency, into custody for questioning following the death of a Chhatra Dal leader who was injured in an attack.

Police said he had been in custody since late Monday night and was being questioned.

Shakil Islam, member secretary of the Gurudaspur pourashava unit of Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal, died at Bangladesh Medical University at around 8:15pm on Monday, 12 days after being critically injured in an attack by assailants. Following his death, police stepped up efforts to identify those responsible for the attack.

Several Chhatra Dal sources said the lawmaker’s two sons have separate groups of followers and supporters, and there is rivalry between the two groups. Shakil, who died after the attack, was a follower of the lawmaker’s younger son, Mahmuduzzaman.

According to police sources, Natore District Detective Branch (DB) police took Nuruzzaman into custody on Monday night following Shakil’s death.

He was initially taken to Gurudaspur Police Station before being transferred to the DB office in Natore district headquarters, where he was questioned.

Abdul Hannan, officer-in-charge (OC) of Gurudaspur Police Station, confirmed that the lawmaker’s son had been taken into police custody for questioning.

Prothom Alo also spoke to Nazrul Islam, an inspector with the Natore District Detective Branch. At around 11:30am on Tuesday, he said, “The matter is under investigation. So, we cannot disclose anything about it at this stage.”

At the time this report was being written, at 1pm on Tuesday, Nuruzzaman was at the Natore DB office. He is a joint convener of the Gurudaspur upazila unit of Jubo Dal. His younger brother, Mahmuduzzaman, is a former joint secretary of the Gurudaspur upazila unit of the BNP.

Shakil Islam, member secretary of the Gurudaspur pourashava unit of Chhatra Dal, was killed following the attack.

Shakil was critically injured when assailants attacked him with sharp weapons at around 10:30pm on 14 October as he was returning from the local Chachkoir Bazar.

Local residents rescued him and took him to the upazila health complex. He was later transferred to Rajshahi and subsequently to Bangladesh Medical Hospital in Dhaka. He died while undergoing treatment at the hospital at around 8:15pm on Monday

Following the attack, Shakil’s father, Rabiul Karim, filed a case with Gurudaspur Police Station on 19 October, accusing eight to 10 unidentified people.

Shakil posted on Facebook about security concerns

On 20 April, Chhatra Dal leader Shakil Islam posted a message on his Facebook account expressing fears for his safety.

“I am very worried about my life. An elder brother has been contacting various circles and groups to have me killed. Apparently, those who can kill me will be paid a large sum of money. I spoke to the OC about this and filed a general diary (GD) at the police station, mentioning their names. If anything happens to me, please file a case based on that GD,” he wrote.

Asked about the Facebook post, Natore district Detective Branch Inspector Nazrul Islam declined to provide details. However, he said the investigation was taking all aspects into consideration.

Abdul Aziz visited the home of Shakil Islam in the Kacharipara area near Gurudaspur upazila headquarters on Tuesday morning.

He offered condolences to Shakil’s father, Rabiul Karim, and other family members.

He also pledged to ensure a proper investigation into the killing and that justice would be served.

Power Grid PLC has formed an investigation committee to determine the cause of the power grid failure that affected a large part of the country on Tuesday.

The committee has been asked to submit its report within the next five working days.

Power went out in eastern Dhaka and parts of Chattogram at around 12.45 pm on Tuesday. Several power plants were shut down following the grid failure. They began restarting one by one about two hours later, and supply gradually increased.

Power outage hits eastern Dhaka, parts of Chattogram; secretariat, BB also without electricity

Power Grid said engineers were working to restore connections in stages to normalise electricity supply. The national grid is operating under the control of the National Load Despatch Centre (NLDC). Major failures have occurred in the national grid before. On 4 October 2022, a failure began in the eastern grid at 2.05 pm, leaving large parts of the country, including Dhaka, Chattogram, Sylhet and Mymensingh, without electricity. Supply was gradually restored over the following three to eight hours.

Earlier, a national grid failure on 1 November 2014 disrupted electricity supply across the country for nearly 12 hours.

item.title: Tarique says Rohingya crisis can only be resolved in Myanmar
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Tuesday said a lasting solution to the Rohingya crisis lies in Myanmar, stressing that forcibly displaced Rohingyas must be able to return to their homeland voluntarily, safely, swiftly and with dignity.
“The lasting solution to the (Rohingya) crisis lies in Myanmar,” he said during a bilateral summit with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi at the Kantei (the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office) in Tokyo.
Tarique expressed deep concerns over the deteriorating situation in Myanmar and the resulting displacement of Rohingya people, said Prime Minister's Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Hossain Shadhin.
He called for an end to all forms of violence, unhindered humanitarian assistance and dialogue among all parties concerned to resolve the crisis.
The prime minister appreciated Japan’s support for Bangladesh’s humanitarian efforts for Rohingyas, who were forcibly displaced from Myanmar’s Rakhine State and took shelter in Bangladesh.
He also urged Japan to remain actively engaged with all parties to help establish peace and stability in Rakhine.
During the summit, the two leaders emphasised strengthening long-standing Bangladesh-Japan relations, expanding trade and investment, and enhancing cooperation in energy security, technology, space research, infrastructure and regional and international affairs.
Tarique Rahman called for greater engagement by the Japanese government and private sector in Bangladesh’s economic development, technological advancement and industrialisation.
He also recalled the visits to Japan by his father, late president Ziaur Rahman, and the contributions of his mother, former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia, to strengthening bilateral ties, pledging to build on their legacy and take relations between the two countries to a new level.
The prime minister highlighted the two countries’ shared commitment to multilateralism, international peace and respect for international law.
He thanked Japan for supporting Bangladesh Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman’s election as president of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.
Tarique expressed his desire to work closely with Japan to strengthen multilateral cooperation and address global challenges during the session.
Reaffirming their shared vision of a free, open, peaceful and inclusive Indo-Pacific, he stressed greater cooperation in regional connectivity, the free flow of trade and economic growth.
Outlining Bangladesh’s ambition to become a regional hub for the economy, technology and manufacturing, the prime minister said the country can become the world’s ninth-largest consumer economy by 2030, while its gross domestic product can exceed US$1 trillion by 2034.
He said Japan holds a special place in the hearts of the people of Bangladesh and recalled that it was among the first countries to recognise Bangladesh after its independence in 1971. Japan has since remained one of Bangladesh’s key development partners for more than five decades.
The bilateral summit between Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi began at 11:45am local time at the Kantei.
The meeting followed a formal welcome at 11:30am, a guard of honour and the introduction of the two leaders’ respective delegations.
During the meeting, Tarique invited Takaichi to visit Bangladesh at a mutually convenient time, expressing hope that the long-standing friendship between the two countries will continue to deepen through mutual trust, cooperation and shared prosperity.

item.title: A bad omen? Syria bans women from university courses
item.description:
Recent changes to university admissions rules in Syria have put a dent in Lin Najab’s plans. The 23-year-old from Damascus is one of the few women at her college studying mechatronics engineering.
“My original plan was to pursue a master’s degree,” Najab told DW. But earlier in October, new rules were announced by Syria’s education ministry regarding two newly created colleges, the National University of Defense Sciences and the Syrian University for Security Sciences. The former now restricts certain courses exclusively to male students, and the latter almost all of them.
These new policies could derail Najab’s plans. “Now I have to start thinking about other options,” she explained. “For example, I might have to move to another province to study.”
It is still possible for Syrian women to study the subjects offered by the two new security institutes, but only at other more generalist universities or colleges.
Moving to another province, away from family, brings other difficulties, Najab continued. Student accommodation in dormitories is uncomfortable, but a woman living alone is still frowned upon by conservative Syrians.
“Even if a girl decides she won’t give up and wants to go study outside her province, her parents will be opposed to the idea, either for security reasons or because we simply don’t want our daughters to go study somewhere else,” said Najab.
The decision to ban women from courses at the new defense and security-related colleges has caused controversy both inside and outside the country.
“Gender doesn’t define ability. It should be about high academic standards, the ones I’m trying to meet,” Najab argued. “In Syria, we need better education and good graduates, so let’s see where the best people are, regardless of gender.”
Fatoun Kharbatli, an activist from Aleppo, is also opposed to the idea of limiting certain subjects to one gender. “A person should choose the field in which they see their abilities as lying,” she told DW. “We were oppressed for 60 years, so now let’s be a nation that keeps pace with global civilization, but without straying from respect and from the basics of our religion.
Qamar al-Yaser, a mother of three in rural Damascus, believes the ban is justified.
The sectors from which women have been excluded “require a strong physique, they need big efforts, travel, organization out in the field and may require staying overnight at remote work sites,” said al-Yaser. “These conditions suit young men more than women.”
A closer look at some of new admission rules indicate they may be less about restricting Syrian women from certain studies and more about keeping them out of the army. For example, attending the National University of Defense Sciences requires that students serve in the Syrian military. Graduates of the University for Security Sciences must also commit to serving up to 20 years with the internal security forces.
Does this mean Syria’s new government is heading in an increasingly restrictive direction when it comes to women’s rights?
Human Rights Watch believes so. A few days after the admissions announcement, the organization released a statement criticizing it. “The discriminatory rules clearly violate Syria’s international legal obligations and are part of a concerning pattern of actions by the transitional authorities that restrict women’s role in state institutions and reinforce gender stereotypes,” the organization said.
Besides the military college bans, there were also other, possibly even more disturbing aspects to the new admissions rules. Restrictions on female students were also applied at a railways institute in Aleppo, oil and gas training organizations in Rmeilan, Homs, Deir el-Zour and Baniyas, and a radio and television course in Idlib. Elsewhere men were barred from kindergarten and nursing school training and midwifery courses. These were to be women-only.
All these come on top of a number of other concerning restrictions and worrying comments by officials. The most recent incident in the education sector involved the government’s alteration of school textbooks for the 2026-2027 academic year.
The education ministry had already announced it would be removing images and symbols associated with the previous authoritarian regime headed by dictator Bashar Assad. But this week journalists also noticed other changes: Pictures of females in the textbooks who had uncovered hair had been removed, or altered so they were now wearing headscarves. A bare-chested statue pictured in one textbook was now wearing a vest. A picture of men dancing was also gone.
Officials have said that some of the gender-exclusionary rules implemented at the new security institutes were actually carried over from the Assad-era colleges that were fused together to create them earlier this year.
Opposition to female soldiers and military leaders isn’t an uncommon attitude in the Middle East’s more conservative circles either. Although many Arab countries allow women to attend military colleges and serve, females are often restricted to non-combat or symbolic roles, a 2024 study by the Washington-based think tank, the Middle East Institute, or MEI, reported.
In Syria, while women have historically participated in the security services, it was “in a limited and largely symbolic capacity,” the Syrian Center for Defense and Security Studies confirmed in a policy paper this year.
But just because an idea is widespread obviously doesn’t make it right, human rights advocates have said.
“Gender diversity in the security sector allows all citizens of a country to be perceived as equal in all aspects of their duties and obligations to the nation state, including defending it,” Dina Arakji, author of the MEI study, argued. “Allowing women to join the military … can advance a society’s perspective on females in nontraditional gender-based roles.”
The admissions ban gives young Syrian women a message about what they can and cannot do, Syrian activist Rana al-Ash argued in a commentary about the ban for Paris-based organization, the Syrian Women’s Political Movement.
“When these messages are reflected in admission requirements, confronting familial and societal expectations becomes even more difficult because the educational institution endorses them,” al-Ash argued.
For Nadra Bunni, a Syrian analyst at the Middle East Institute Switzerland, it’s still unclear as to whether “gender-based restrictions will become a feature of the new Syria.”
But the anger over the admissions ban also raises another important question, she noted. “Will Syria’s new authorities institutionalize an expectation that government decisions can be questioned and potentially reversed,” she asked in a commentary for the online publication, Syria In Transition. “Or [will they] teach citizens that their voices carry little consequence?”

item.title: Zahed: BNP won’t back extrajudicial killings
item.description:
The BNP fought against enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings over the past 17 years and will not backtrack on that position after forming the government, Prime Minister’s Information and Broadcasting Adviser Zahed Ur Rahman said on Tuesday, adding that the prime minister will take the final decision about the inspector general of police over his crossfire remarks.
“If a state or government kills someone extrajudicially, it ceases to function as a state and behaves like a thug,” Zahed said while speaking at a press briefing on the progress of various government activities at the Secretariat.
No democratic government can support extrajudicial killings, he said, stressing that the state must arrest criminals and hand them over to the judicial system for trial.
“Anyone can commit murder. A state becomes a state when it exercises the authority to deliver justice,” he added.
A death sentence can be imposed through judicial proceedings, but extrajudicial killing can never be an act of the state, the adviser said, adding that the state can arrest an accused person and hand them over to the judiciary, exercising the executive authority and laws can be amended, if necessary, but there can be no scope for extrajudicial killings.
He said the government has no intention of remaining in power after its five-year term through night-time voting or dummy elections. “It will, therefore, avoid any action that can damage its credibility, as incidents such as extrajudicial killings will undermine public confidence in the government.”
Asked about IGP Md Ali Hossain Fakir’s remarks that crossfire operations could be carried out if the government gives permission, Zahed said he believed the police chief retreated from his earlier position in subsequent remarks. “He also stepped back from serious allegations he made about journalists in general,” he said, adding that he thought the issue should now be put to rest.
Asked whether the IGP should be allowed to remain in office even after clarifying his remarks, he said the matter is for journalists to assess.
The adviser said he felt the situation would have been problematic had the police chief continued to stand by his earlier statement.
He also stressed that government officials are not obliged to carry out illegal orders and public servants must perform their duties in accordance with the law.
Zahed also said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will take the final decision about the IGP after returning from the Japan visit.
Responding to a question about the arrest of a woman entrepreneur in Bhaluka, Mymensingh, for regretting voting for the BNP on Facebook live, he said he did not consider the position taken by local BNP activists who protested against her remarks to be justified.
Police took the woman into custody following the protests and later sent her to court under Section 151 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Zahed said people have the right to express such views. “Many people in Bangladesh, including some who make offensive remarks about the Prime Minister, are expressing their opinions without facing similar action,” he said, adding that such remarks can certainly be made.
He, however, said the matter is now within the jurisdiction of the judiciary, expressing hope that investigators will not treat the woman’s remarks as a criminal offence.
Asked about the reported vandalism and looting of the homes of three Hindu families in Pirganj, Rangpur, the adviser said he heard that police were deployed and action was taken in this regard.
He said there was a tendency among some extremist groups in Bangladesh to act aggressively. “Such tendencies increased during the interim government’s tenure, and appropriate action was not taken against such incidents in many cases,” he added.
Zahed also assured that the current government will take action against such crimes. “You cannot expect to remain beyond the reach of justice under this government. I assure you of that,” he said.
Members of the Hindu community also want to live safely in a liberal democratic country, he said, adding that people have expectations from political parties entrusted with governing the country, and the BNP will have to fulfil those expectations.

item.title: HC gives task force six more months to probe Sagar-Runi murder
item.description:
The High Court has granted a task force investigating the murders of journalist couple Sagar Sarowar and Meherun Runi another six months to complete its probe.
The court also summoned the task force chief and Tanvir Zoha, an information technology expert and prosecutor at the International Crimes Tribunal, to provide an update on the investigation on April 27 next year. They have been directed to appear with relevant documents, and the court will hear their statements in camera.
A High Court bench comprising Justice Shikder Md Mahmudur Razi and Justice Fatema Anwar passed the order on Tuesday.
Senior lawyers Monzil Morshed and Shishir Manir appeared for the couple's family, while Attorney General Ruhul Quddus Kazal represented the state.
On September 30, 2024, the High Court ordered the removal of the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) from the investigation and directed the formation of a high-level task force under the Ministry of Home Affairs. The court set April 6, 2025, as the deadline for submitting the investigation report.
The ministry subsequently formed the task force. However, the investigation did not progress as scheduled, as the High Court was on vacation on the designated date. The state later sought additional time, and the case was placed on the High Court's hearing list again.
Sagar, news editor of Maasranga Television, and Runi, a senior reporter at ATN Bangla, were murdered at their rented apartment in the capital's West Rajabazar area on the night of February 11, 2012. Their only son, Mahir Sarowar Megh, was at home at the time.
Runi's brother, Nausher Ali Roman, filed a murder case with Sher-e-Bangla Nagar police station. Local police initially investigated the case before it was transferred to the Detective Branch three days later.
After the Detective Branch failed to make progress, the case was handed over to RAB on April 18, 2012.

item.title: Power outage hits Secretariat, key areas of Dhaka
item.description:
A fault in the Meghnaghat-Haripur national grid line disrupted electricity supply to the Secretariat, several areas of Dhaka and parts of Chittagong on Tuesday.
The outage occurred at 12:43pm, leaving several areas of the capital without electricity.
Power Grid Bangladesh said the disruption affected areas including Bhulta, Haripur, Siddhirganj, Gulshan, Rampura, Ullon and Motijheel. Parts of Chittagong also experienced power cuts.
An official responsible for electricity at the Public Works Ministry in the Secretariat said the Dhaka Power Distribution Company Limited (DPDC) had informed him that the outage was caused by a grid failure.
Power Grid Bangladesh said the technical cause of the outage was yet to be determined. Restoration work was underway, with engineers reconnecting affected areas in phases. The national grid system is under the supervision of the National Load Despatch Centre (NLDC).
In an emergency press release, the Power Division said efforts were underway to restore electricity supply. Power was gradually returning to affected areas, with full restoration expected shortly.
Power Grid Bangladesh later announced that restoration of the national grid had been completed at 2:30pm, with all grid lines and substations operational.
The agency said electricity supply remained normal in the northern parts of the country and other unaffected areas.
Several areas of the capital, including the Secretariat and its surroundings, Moghbazar, Modhubagh, Shantinagar, Malibagh and Khilgaon, were reported to be without electricity.
In an emergency press release issued on Tuesday, the Power Division said a technical fault had disrupted electricity supply to parts of Dhaka and Chitttagong, adding that urgent efforts were underway to restore power.
Power plants were being brought back online in phases, and scattered load-shedding was expected to ease as electricity generation increased, the agency said.
It apologised for the temporary inconvenience caused by the unexpected power disruption.

item.title: UCB, Mastercard and GP unveils co-branded sticker payment card
item.description:
United Commercial Bank PLC (UCB), Mastercard and Grameenphone on Tuesday unveiled a co-branded sticker payment card, offering consumers in Bangladesh a simple and convenient way to make contactless payments while enjoying cashback, rewards and exclusive lifestyle benefits.
The event was attended by Brent T Christensen, US Ambassador to Bangladesh, as chief guest.
Also present were Sharif Zahir, chairman, UCB; Mohammad Mamdudur Rashid, chief executive officer, UCB; Gautam Aggarwal, division president, India & South Asia, Mastercard; Sandun Hapugoda, country manager, Sri Lanka, Maldives, Bangladesh, Bhutan & Nepal, Mastercard; Zakia Sultana, country manager, Bangladesh, Mastercard; Solaiman Alam, chief product officer, Grameenphone, along with senior executives from the three organizations.
The prepaid sticker card can be attached to a smartphone or another suitable item, allowing cardholders to make payments by simply tapping it on a contactless-enabled point-of-sale (POS) terminal.
This eliminates the need to carry a conventional payment card, making everyday transactions quicker and easier.
The card combines UCB’s banking services, Mastercard’s secure payment technology and Grameenphone’s MyGP digital ecosystem, enabling cardholders to enjoy seamless payments alongside a range of other benefits.
Cardholders can avail 10% cashback on eligible OTT and bundle purchases from MyGP, MyGP Shop transactions and learning courses, along with 3% cashback on eligible GPFI subscriptions.
They can also claim Tk50 cashback on eligible roaming pack purchases, exclusive offers at GPStar and Mastercard partner merchants, and accelerated MyGP Points on qualifying transactions.
All cashback offers are subject to the applicable terms and conditions.
Sharif Zahir, chairman, UCB, said: “This collaboration reflects UCB’s commitment to delivering innovative financial solutions that meet the evolving needs of customers. By bringing together banking, connectivity and global payments technology, the sticker payment card provides a seamless, convenient and rewarding way to make every day digital payments.”
Gautam Aggarwal, division president, India & South Asia, Mastercard, said: “The future of payments lies in making transactions effortless, secure and seamlessly integrated into consumers’ daily routines. Through this collaboration, we are introducing an innovative form factor that expands consumer choice while supporting the continued growth of contactless payments in Bangladesh.”
The card comes with a first-year fee waiver, while the annual fee will be waived for cardholders spending Tk100,000 or more in a calendar year.
Solaiman Alam, chief product officer, Grameenphone, said: “As consumers increasingly embrace digital lifestyles, they are looking for payment solutions that are simple, convenient and relevant to their everyday needs. The sticker payment card brings payments closer to the digital experiences our customers already use through MyGP. This association reflects our commitment to creating greater value for people through digital innovation.”
The introduction of co-branded sticker payment card reflects the shared commitment of UCB, Mastercard and Grameenphone to accelerating the adoption of contactless payments and making digital transactions more secure and rewarding for consumers across Bangladesh.

item.title: Sajek residents demand probe into attack on blockade
item.description:
Sajek residents and local organizations have demanded punishment for those responsible for an alleged attack on a peaceful road blockade on October 22, compensation for affected traders and withdrawal of a case against protesters.
In a memorandum submitted to the government on Monday, the Sajek Public Rights Protection Committee and Sajek Karbari Association also demanded an impartial judicial inquiry into the incident and the removal of armed members of the Santu Larma-led faction of the Parbatya Chattagram Jana Samhati Samiti (PCJSS) from the area, said a press release.
The signatories alleged that the armed group had been threatening residents, firing indiscriminately and extorting money from Jhum cultivators, creating fear and insecurity in several villages.
According to the statement, the group began armed activities in the area on August 31. Its members allegedly demanded Tk1,000 for every ari of Jhum land and extorted money from owners of rice-processing machines, turmeric-grinding machines and engine-powered boats. A nine-year-old girl, Kosmita Tripura, was reportedly injured by gunfire.
Residents said they had repeatedly urged the local military administration to take action against the group but received no effective response. They began an indefinite road blockade on October 11, temporarily suspending it after the army sought additional time. The blockade resumed on October 15, was suspended for Durga Puja and restarted on October 22.
The signatories alleged that security personnel attacked protesters with batons without provocation while discussions were underway about allowing stranded tourists to pass. Army personnel subsequently opened fire, vandalised and looted shops and homes in Ujopazar, and injured several people, they claimed.
They also alleged that army and police personnel later attempted to arrest SSC examinee Jharna Chakma over her participation in the blockade.
The memorandum was signed by Babudhan Chakma, convener of the Sajek Public Rights Protection Committee; Natun Joy Chakma, president of the Sajek Karbari Association; Ushatan Chakma of the Student-People's Struggle Council; Jiko Chakma of the Sajek Public Rights Protection Committee; and Sadhana Debi Chakma of Sajek Women's Society.

item.title: Man beaten to death over alleged mugging in Jatrabari, another injured
item.description:

The deceased was identified as Joni, 32, son of the late Abul Kashem, from Matbor Goli in the Kazlarpar area of Jatrabari.
The injured, Nisat Miah, 27, son of Mohsin Miah from the Kalapatti area of Jatrabari, is currently undergoing treatment at Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH) under police custody.
According to police, the incident took place between 7am and 8am near Gate No-4 of Bibir Bagicha on Demra Road under Jatrabari Police Station.
Jatrabari Police Station Sub-Inspector (SI) Md Hasan said a group of youths was allegedly committing muggings in the area in the morning when local residents chased them.
While others managed to flee, locals caught Joni and Nisat and beat them up, leaving Joni dead on the spot.
Upon receiving information, police recovered Joni's body from the scene and sent it to the DMCH morgue for an autopsy after completing legal formalities.
Police said legal proceedings regarding the incident are underway.

item.title: Coco peat trial explores soil-free farming in Gazipur
item.description:
No ploughing, no soil beds and no conventional land preparation. Instead, rows of polybags filled with coco peat, a growing medium made from coconut husks, are nurturing cucumber plants in Sapmara village of Gazipur. As the plants grow, so does farmer Ferdous Mia's hope that crops can be cultivated successfully without soil.
Ferdous is not pursuing a large commercial venture. His initiative is a small-scale experiment to assess the feasibility of soil-free farming under local conditions, including its production potential, ease of cultivation and overall costs.
The experiment is underway on three kathas of land in Sapmara village in Pubail, Gazipur city. Known locally for his enthusiasm for farming, Ferdous has long cultivated papaya and various traditional vegetables. He has now turned to soilless cultivation in search of an alternative approach to farming.
He is receiving guidance from Ariful Islam, a Bangladeshi expatriate farmer who gained experience in coco peat-based cultivation in Malaysia. Together, they are exploring how the technique can be adapted to local conditions.
In the first phase, Ferdous has installed 200 polybags filled with coco peat instead of soil. Made from processed coconut husks and fibres, the material provides a growing medium that retains moisture, allows air to reach plant roots and supports nutrient management. Cucumber plants are now growing in the bags.
"I am interested in adopting new and modern technologies alongside conventional farming. That is why I have started soil-free cultivation using coco peat. Although the initial cost is somewhat higher, I hope the expenses will come down if production becomes regular," Ferdous said.
Soilless cultivation is not new to global agriculture. Techniques such as hydroponics and coco peat-based growing systems are used in various countries, particularly where farmland is limited and growers seek to make more efficient use of available space.
For Ferdous, however, the immediate challenge is to determine whether the method can deliver practical and economic benefits in Bangladesh. He is monitoring the plants' growth, water requirements, nutrient needs and susceptibility to pests and diseases. The decisive test will be the yield and whether it justifies the investment.
If the experiment proves successful, he plans to extend the method to other fruits and vegetables. He believes soil-free cultivation could help increase production in limited spaces at a time when agricultural land is shrinking and farmers face seasonal challenges.
"Technology is playing an increasingly important role in agriculture. If the experiment succeeds, we can try to produce more in a smaller space. I plan to work with other crops as well," he said.
With pressure on agricultural land mounting and food demand remaining high, finding ways to increase production within limited spaces has become increasingly important. Yet growing crops in coco peat does not automatically guarantee higher yields or greater profits.
The method's viability will depend on several factors, including initial investment, the cost of coco peat and other inputs, labour requirements, nutrient management and the quantity and quality of the harvest. Ferdous's experiment could offer a small but useful insight into how the technique performs under local conditions.
Farmers in Sapmara are also watching the cucumber plants grow in the coco peat-filled bags, and the initiative has sparked curiosity about the alternative technique. If the trial succeeds, it could encourage others in the area to explore technology-based cultivation.
Kaliganj Upazila Agriculture Officer Hasibul Hasan said seedlings produced using coco peat were of good quality and less susceptible to diseases.
He described coco peat-based cultivation as a potential tool for improving farmers' livelihoods, adding that proper crop management and the use of improved technology could help increase their financial returns.

item.title: Article 9 Committee launched to ensure accessibility for persons with disabilities
item.description:
A new advocacy platform, the Article 9 Committee, has been launched to promote the implementation of Article 9 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD), which requires measures to ensure accessibility for persons with disabilities across all areas of life.
The committee held its inaugural meeting at the Omni Residency Hotel in Baridhara, Dhaka, on Monday, with a focus on addressing barriers in infrastructure, transport, information and communication technology, and public services.
The meeting was organized by the women-led Bangladesh Society for the Change and Advocacy Nexus (B-SCAN), with support from the Centre for Services and Information on Disability (CSID) and the Centre for Disabilities in Development (CDD), under the Disability Inclusive Civic Engagement (DiCE) project. The project is supported by the Nagorikata – Civic Engagement Fund, managed by GFA.
Article 9 of the UNCRPD calls on states to ensure that persons with disabilities can access the physical environment, transportation, information and communications, and other facilities and services open or provided to the public on an equal basis with others. Accessibility is essential to independent living and full participation in society.
Representatives attend the inaugural meeting of the Article 9 Committee, formed to promote accessibility for persons with disabilities, in Baridhara, Dhaka, on Monday, October 26, 2026. Photo: Courtesy
The committee aims to raise awareness of accessibility rights, bring together organisations of persons with disabilities, civil society groups, development organisations, professional bodies and academic institutions, and strengthen coordination and accountability in implementing accessibility standards.
Accessibility extends beyond ramps to include accessible buildings and toilets, public transport, websites, sign language and information in accessible formats. Universal design can also benefit older people, children, pregnant women and those with temporary mobility difficulties.
B-SCAN Executive Director Salma Mahbub said the platform would work nationally to make Bangladesh accessible to all by combining the knowledge and experience of civil society organisations.
The committee's initial priorities include identifying barriers across infrastructure, transport, communication technologies and services; engaging responsible institutions; and advocating for universal design to make accessibility an integral part of planning and service delivery.
Representatives from B-SCAN, CDD and CSID attended the meeting, alongside those from WaterAid, Bangladesh Poribesh Andolon (BAPA), the Bangladesh Institute of Planners (BIP), Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST), BRAC, Friendship, SERAC, WBB Trust, the Women with Disabilities Development Foundation (WDDF), SMF, the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FBCCI), and Mass Studio.

item.title: Persons with disabilities demand immediate anti-discrimination law
item.description:
Persons with disabilities and rights advocates have urged the government to immediately enact a comprehensive anti-discrimination law to ensure inclusion, protection and equal rights for all marginalized communities.
The call came at a consultation organized jointly by the Centre for Disabilities in Development (CDD) and Manusher Jonno Foundation (MJF) at the Shakti Foundation Training and Research Center in Akran, Savar, on Tuesday.
Held under the Disability Inclusive Civic Engagement (DiCE) project, the consultation brought together persons with disabilities, civil society representatives and government officials to review the draft Anti-Discrimination Bill and propose recommendations from a disability rights perspective.
The project is funded by Switzerland, Canada and the European Union, implemented through GFA Consulting Group GmbH and supported by the Nagorikata – Civic Engagement Fund.
Wasiur Rahman Tonmoy, lead – Youth & Social Cohesion at MJF, presented the keynote paper, outlining discrimination faced by marginalized groups in education, healthcare, employment and public and private services. These groups include Dalits, Indigenous people in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, tea garden workers and persons with disabilities.
KM Shahiduzzaman, upazila social services officer in Savar, attended as chief guest and stressed the need for enforceable legal protections and coordination between government agencies and non-governmental organisations to improve access to essential services.
Advocate Ruma Sultana, programme coordinator at MJF, highlighted the need for continued consultations with diverse communities to refine the proposed legislation. She was involved in drafting the initial Anti-Discrimination Bill, 2022.
Umme Farhana Zarif Kanta, deputy director and team lead for PROKAS at Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST), called for stronger partnerships with grassroots organizations to ensure persons with disabilities are represented in legislative advocacy.
The consultation included 48 persons with disabilities: 25 with visual impairments, 14 with physical disabilities, seven with hearing impairments and two with cerebral palsy. Sign language interpretation was provided by Iftekhar Ahmed Shorful.
Facilitated by Tonmoy, participants worked in five groups to review the draft bill and develop recommendations.
They called for the legislation to be enacted under the title “Anti-Discrimination Law” and for its definitions of discrimination to be aligned with existing national laws and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD).
Other recommendations included incorporating relevant provisions of the Rights and Protection of Persons with Disabilities Act 2013 into the proposed law, ensuring representation of persons with disabilities on monitoring committees and the proposed National Anti-Discrimination Commission, and simplifying complaint procedures and access to legal aid.
Participants also called for effective enforcement and accountability mechanisms covering both public and private sectors.
Anika Rahman Lipy, assistant director of training at CDD, delivered the closing remarks and vote of thanks. Participants pledged to continue engaging with policymakers to advance the proposed law.

item.title: Man jailed for embezzling Tk6 crore in Rajuk plot scam
item.description:
A Dhaka court has sent Munshi Manzur-e-Elahi, also known as Manjurul Alam, to jail after rejecting his bail petition in a case over the alleged embezzlement of Tk6.23 crore from a businessman by promising to arrange a five-katha Rajuk plot in Uttara.
Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Md Zakir Hossain passed the order on Tuesday. Abdulllah Al Mamun, a lawyer for the complainant, confirmed the matter.
According to the case statement, the complainant, Md Nasir, proprietor of Prashanti Enterprise, knew the accused and had been involved in a joint land trading business with them in Dhaka.
Under an oral agreement, Nasir was entitled to 50% of the profits from land sales, with the remaining half going to the accused.
The accused allegedly told Nasir that a five-katha Rajuk plot was available in Uttara for Tk5–6 crore and could later be sold for Tk9–10 crore. Persuaded by the offer, Nasir visited the plot on August 1, 2023, and agreed to invest.
The complaint alleges that the accused subsequently collected Tk6.23 crore from Nasir in instalments through pay orders and cash, claiming the money was needed for the advance payment and registration of the land.
Several crore taka were transferred through pay orders issued by City Bank and IFIC Bank in favour of Md Robiul Alam, proprietor of Rafin Enterprise, and another accused, Munshi Manzur-e-Elahi.
Other alleged members of the group, including Rafiqul Islam, Md Anisur Rahman Mia Hasib, Hasna Hena and Asif Hasan Tulip, also collected cash from Nasir at different times, according to the complaint.
Despite receiving the money, the accused allegedly delayed handing over the plot. They later stopped answering Nasir's calls and vacated their office in Sector 16 of Uttara after locking it, the complaint says.
When Nasir sought a refund on December 1, 2024, the accused allegedly refused to return the money.
Nasir filed a Complaint Register (CR) case with the court on December 29, 2024. The court took cognisance of the case the same day and directed the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) to investigate. Following the investigation, the CID submitted its report on June 30 this year.
Meanwhile, victims formed a human chain on the court premises from Tuesday morning until afternoon, demanding Manjurul Alam's trial.
They also called for the swift arrest of other alleged members of the fraud syndicate, the recovery of the money and stronger intervention by the authorities.
