item.title: Sagar and Runi remained alive for some time despite injuries: What the investigation has revealed so far
item.description:
Neither journalist Sagar Sarwar nor his wife, Meherun Runi, had significant injuries to vital organs. The nature of the killings does not appear consistent with the work of professional killers. Both victims had multiple wounds that caused substantial blood loss. However, it appears that they remained alive for a considerable time after being injured. 

There were signs of injuries on their necks and backs, as well as below their eyes. The crime scene and the extent of the victims’ injuries suggest that the killers were not in a hurry.

These observations are included in the “Special Observations” section of a progress report on the investigation into the Sagar–Runi murder case, prepared by a high-powered task force comprising experienced officials from various agencies. The observations are based on the inquest and post-mortem reports.

The report was presented on Tuesday before a High Court bench comprising Justices Shikder Mahmudur Razi and Fatema Anwar. Following a request from the state for more time to complete the investigation, the court granted a further six months. 29 April has been set for the next order.

DNA of 2 unidentified men found

According to preliminary DNA test results cited in the progress report, DNA profiles belonging to two unidentified men were found in samples collected from the bedsheet used to restrain Sagar Sarowar and from Meherun Runi’s T-shirt.

The report says attempts were made at two US laboratories that specialise in DNA analysis to identify the unknown perpetrators and develop images of them. However, these efforts were unsuccessful because the DNA samples contained a high degree of mixing, making it impossible to establish a match. Investigators also checked whether the unidentified DNA matched that of any suspects or accused persons identified during the investigation.

According to the progress report, knives, a boti (a traditional cutting blade), knife handles, clothing worn by Sagar and Runi, other evidence seized in connection with the killings, and buccal swab samples from 25 individuals were sent to several laboratories abroad for DNA testing. Reports from the laboratories found no match between the DNA recovered from the evidence and the samples submitted from those individuals.

A review of the reports found DNA from a total of four people at the crime scene: three men and one woman. One of the male profiles was identified as belonging to Sagar Sarwar, while the female profile was identified as belonging to Meherun Nahar Runi. The identities of the other two men remain unknown.

Despite the lengthy investigation, the motive for the killings and the identities of those responsible have yet to be conclusively established.

No link found to family or professional disputes

The progress report says investigators found no evidence that one spouse killed the other because of family or marital discord and that the surviving spouse then died by suicide. Nor did they find evidence suggesting that the murders were connected to the couple’s professional work.

The couple had lived in Germany for an extended period and returned to Bangladesh seven months before their deaths. Investigators spoke to senior colleagues at Sagar’s workplace, private television channel Maashranga Television, but found no evidence of professional enmity or disputes involving him.

The report notes that construction of the Summit Bibiyana Power Plant began in 2013 and that the plant started operations in 2015. As construction and operations began after the couple’s deaths, investigators found no connection between the killings and the Summit Group.

Investigators also found no evidence that the murders were linked to financial disputes or land-related conflicts. Inquiries at the couple’s ancestral village found no evidence of any land dispute with others. No evidence was found to suggest that marital discord had led to the killings.

Mobile phones and laptops still missing

The progress report describes the Sagar–Runi murders as a high-profile case and says that a task force comprising officials from the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI), Criminal Investigation Department (CID), Police Headquarters and Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) has still been unable to recover the mobile phones stolen during the crime and the couple’s two laptops.

Investigators have also been unable to question several former officials in connection with the case. 

They include former Inspector General of Police Hasan Mahmud Khandaker, former Dhaka Metropolitan Police Detective Branch chief Monirul Islam, who served as a media spokesperson on the murder case, former RAB Director General Mokhlesur Rahman, and former Home Minister Mohiuddin Khan Alamgir.

Journalist Rumi Noman has been questioned and his statement recorded. Efforts to question others are continuing.

The report says questioning the individuals mentioned above could potentially provide important information or new leads in the investigation.

How Ziaul Ahsan and Rokeya Prachi came under scrutiny

The progress report says that on 30 August, prosecutor Tanvir Hasan Zoha of the tribunal told various electronic media outlets and social media platforms that the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) had conducted a raid at the Barishal residence of retired Major General Ziaul Ahsan, a former director of the National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre (NTMC). The ACC reportedly seized several pieces of digital evidence, including printed records of geolocation data, SMS messages and call detail records (CDRs).

An orderly serving in the armed forces was questioned in connection with the matter. Zoha said that preliminary investigations had indicated possible links between Major General Ziaul Ahsan and a media personality and the Sagar–Runi murders.

International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) Chief Prosecutor Md Aminul Islam made similar statements to electronic media outlets and on social media, supporting Zoha’s remarks. He said the findings would be handed over to PBI investigators once their investigation was complete.

The progress report further says that, during discussions with task force members, ICT Chief Prosecutor Aminul Islam and prosecutor Tanvir Hasan Zoha stated that their preliminary investigation had found possible links between the murders and retired Major General Ziaul Ahsan and media personality Rokeya Prachi. They said they were investigating and verifying the information and would hand over their findings to the PBI investigating officer after completing their preliminary inquiry.

The task force has remained in contact with the ICT prosecutors. It also sent a letter to the chief prosecutor on 13 October 2026, requesting that the digital evidence and information held by the tribunal be handed over for the investigation. The report says those materials have not yet been received.

The progress report says more time is needed to complete the investigation, uncover the full circumstances of the killings, identify and arrest those responsible, recover the stolen property, examine and verify the information received by the ICT, and question witnesses.

Murders and the case: A 14-year timeline

On 11 February 2012, journalist couple Sagar Sarwar and Meherun Runi were murdered at their rented apartment in West Rajabazar in the capital. At the time, Sagar worked for private television channel Maashranga Television, while Runi worked for ATN Bangla.

Runi’s brother, Nausher Alam, filed a murder case at Sher-e-Bangla Nagar police station. The Detective Branch of police initially investigated the case. Following a writ petition, the High Court ordered on 18 April 2012 that the investigation be handed over to RAB.

In September 2024, the Home Secretary filed an application with the High Court seeking a modification of the order assigning the case to RAB. After hearing the matter, the court on 30 September 2024 directed the formation of a high-powered task force comprising experienced officials from various agencies to investigate the Sagar–Runi murder case. It also ordered that an investigation report be submitted to the court within six months of the completion of the investigation. A high-powered task force was subsequently formed.

The case came before the court again on 22 April last year. Citing the ongoing investigation and progress made, the state sought nine months to complete the work. The court granted six months.

The matter was brought before the court again on 23 October last year. In response to another request for more time from the state, the court granted a further six months.

The case was then listed for an order on 26 April this year. The state sought more time, and the court granted another six months.

The matter came up for an order again on Tuesday. The state once more requested an extension. The court granted a further six months and set 29 April for the next order. This is the fourth time the task force has been granted an extension.

At the hearing, Attorney General Md Ruhul Quddus Kajal presented parts of the report on behalf of the state. Additional Attorney General Mohammad Arshadur Rouf and Deputy Attorney General Nur Mohammad Azmi were also present.

Senior lawyer Manzil Morshed represented the petitioner, while senior lawyer Mohammad Shishir Monir appeared on behalf of the complainant.

item.title: Netanyahu and rival each claim mandate after tight Israel election
item.description:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and rival Gadi Eisenkot each vowed on Wednesday (28 October) to form a government after both came up short in the first election since the 7 October, 2023 attack.

Voters turned out Tuesday in the highest numbers in decades to give their verdict on the divisive rule of Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister who has pushed the country sharply to the right and unleashed a wave of wars in response to the Hamas attack.

Exit polls showed Eisenkot, a former military chief and political novice, and his opposition bloc neck and neck with Netanyahu's hard-right camp and both well away from the threshold for a majority in parliament.

The strongest gains came from Arab Israeli parties whose voters turned out in soaring numbers against Netanyahu, who has relentlessly warned that the minority would dilute the Jewish nationalist direction in which he has taken Israel.

Netanyahu, greeting cheering supporters at a Jerusalem convention centre after 3:00 am (0100 GMT), called for a "strong government of the right" and said that the "Jewish and Zionist majority must unite".

The 77-year-old prime minister was unusually brief and did not directly claim victory.

Instead, he listed leaders Israel has killed under his orders and again hinted that he was ready for a third bombing campaign against Iran alongside US President Donald Trump, his close ally.

"Israel has a unique opportunity with our partner President Trump to forever eliminate the existential threat of Iran," Netanyahu said.

Eisenkot, speaking to his own supporters in Tel Aviv, issued a veiled warning to Netanyahu, who observers say could use a war to push for a unity government.

"Netanyahu, don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.

Addressing Israel's security establishment, Eisenkot said that they served the state and not Netanyahu, calling him "a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate or the people's trust".

'Public has voted for change'

Eisenkot shares many of Netanyahu's views on security and has backed the Gaza offensive following 7 October that has reduced the territory to rubble.

But Eisenkot has vowed to create a more inclusive atmosphere inside Israel and to rein in extremist settlers in the West Bank who have attacked Palestinians with virtual impunity.

After turnout of nearly 78 per cent, the highest since 1999, Eisenkot said it would be a mistake to hold a second election and vowed to work "swiftly" to form a government.

"The public has voted for change," Eisenkot said. "A worthy leader would accept the people's vote of no confidence and announce his retirement from political life today."

The three mainstream Israeli television networks in exit polls gave the two blocs each around 51 seats -- well below the 61 needed to govern -- after initially giving an edge to the opposition.

Israeli Arab lists were projected to win 17 to 18 seats, a sharp gain, with some Israeli Arab communities reporting near-universal turnout driven by outrage to often derogatory rhetoric against them by Netanyahu's far-right allies.

Key Israeli Arab leader Mansour Abbas said he believed the right had "suffered a major loss" and was open to working with Eisenkot.

But Eisenkot said during the campaign he would not govern with Israeli Arab lawmakers -- and Netanyahu again suggested that a government relying on Arab votes would lack legitimacy.

Arab lawmakers could give Eisenkot support in parliamentary votes to maintain a minority government without joining a coalition. If not, Israel could head to new elections.

Itamar Ben Gvir, a far-right firebrand who according to exit polls did not gain as much as many expected, warned Netanyahu against another option -- a unity government with Eisenkot.

"It would be a terrible mistake," said Ben Gvir, who champions the expulsion of Palestinians and would likely be excluded from any unity government.

Hebrew University of Jerusalem political scientist Gideon Rahat said Ben Gvir had succeeded in mobilising votes -- of Israeli Arabs.

But he said: "Even if Netanyahu lost, that doesn't mean Eisenkot won."

Divisive

The election came as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by the war in Iran and the military campaign in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank.

Netanyahu himself faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court over Gaza as well as domestic corruption charges that could land him in prison if he loses power.

Eisenkot is a political novice whose mild manner is the antithesis of the smooth-talking incumbent.

The son of working-class Moroccan Jewish immigrants, Eisenkot would be the first prime minister of Middle Eastern or North African descent.

Before voting, the 66-year-old Eisenkot paid his respects privately at the grave of his son Gal, whose death fighting in Gaza has drawn empathy from many Israelis.

Tens of thousands of Israelis are estimated to have flown in from abroad for an election seen as crucial for their country.

Eilana Zisblit, 55, told AFP she had travelled back from Canada, where she has lived for almost 30 years, to vote for a centre-right party in Eisenkot's bloc.

"The country is going in a really, really bad direction. Both for Jews and Arabs living in the country, and for Jews living abroad," she said.

The time to act is "now, or the country really won't survive anymore".

item.title: In defence of speculators: Don’t shoot the market’s shock absorbers
item.description:
In public debates on economic stress, market speculation is quickly condemned as an act of financial sabotage. In Bangladesh, this view is very common. Commentators often describe speculators as bad actors. They blame them for falling share prices and dollar shortages. Blaming speculators targets the messenger instead of the problem. Informed speculators provide essential services. They create ongoing liquidity and absorb financial shocks.

Real-economy participants do not trade every day. A factory sells foreign exchange only when export payments arrive. A bank buys government debt only when surplus deposits build up. If markets depended solely on direct end-users, trading would slow down. An exporter wanting to sell dollars in the morning would have to wait for an importer wanting the same amount at that exact moment. This delay would widen trading spreads and cause sharp price jumps.

Speculators remove this friction by taking on price risk for profit. They narrow spreads and lower transaction costs for businesses. In doing so, they create steady secondary-market trading. Without secondary-market liquidity, primary markets stall. Developing new financial products then becomes impossible.

The structural trap: How banking arbitrage starves our capital market

Stagnation of new financial products

Over the past few decades, our market has witnessed several innovative debt instruments. Issuers have introduced zero-coupon bonds, microcredit securitizations, corporate debentures, and bank Tier 2 capital bonds. Yet, these innovations rarely developed into active, self-sustaining asset classes.

Without speculative participants trading in the secondary market, these instruments failed to achieve repeat commercial value. Institutional buyers treated them as buy-and-hold private placements, locking them away until maturity. As a result, product development relied uncomfortably on fiscal concessions and regulatory mandates. Authorities resorted to special tax exemptions, mandatory investment quotas, and waivers from single-borrower legal lending limits. When an instrument requires regulatory life support rather than active market pricing to survive, the product line inevitably stagnates.

Missing derivatives and the hedging void

This liquidity shortage shows up clearly in foreign exchange and money markets. A healthy forward market needs active trading in both spot foreign exchange and interbank lending. Without two-way flow in these basic cash markets, banks cannot price forward contracts accurately.
When forward markets fail, the entire derivative structure breaks down. Useful tools like currency options and interest rate swaps need an active forward curve.

This gap causes trouble across all asset classes. In the bond market, thin trading prevents clear pricing, so companies struggle to issue long-term debt. In the stock market, the lack of hedging tools forces investors to rely only on rising prices. Foreign direct investment and portfolio investment suffer as well. Global funds must manage currency risk. When an economy lacks basic hedging tools, foreign capital faces steep uncertainty. Global investors then demand extreme risk premiums or take their capital elsewhere.

Regulatory lobbying as a substitute for hedging

When markets lack standard risk tools, companies still look for protection. Lobbying regulators then becomes the main hedging strategy for local businesses.

Firms do not buy forward contracts or execute swaps. Instead, they ask authorities for special policy help. They seek interest rate caps, special exchange rates, and loan delay packages.

This habit harms market discipline. Political influence replaces proper risk management. Meanwhile, the actual financial risks remain in the system.

The real cost of squeezing speculation

A thin market dominated by passive investors invites price cartels. In contrast, well-funded independent traders deter market abuse. When an insider tries to distort an asset price, opposing traders sell against that distortion and help restore normal levels.

Bangladesh showed the danger of ignoring this balance with equity floor prices. The policy tried to stop paper losses, but it drove speculative money away and stopped two-way trading on the Dhaka Stock Exchange. Buyers vanished, portfolios were trapped, turnover fell hard, and normal investment stopped. Halting regular trade does not protect an exchange; it simply freezes it.

In a functional market, speculators act as shock absorbers by stepping in to buy battered stocks when panicked long-term investors rush for the exit. Because speculators have shorter investment horizons, they are willing to warehouse falling assets to capture short-term rebounds. Their willingness to buy on down days establishes a natural price floor, provides an immediate exit for sellers, and keeps turnover moving.

The foreign exchange crisis of 2022 and 2023 demonstrated the exact same failure. Facing acute dollar shortages, authorities blamed bank treasuries and currency dealers for speculative hoarding. Officials imposed rigid caps and set multiple artificial exchange rates for exporters, remitters, and importers. By suppressing normal market-making and trading margins, the policy paralysed the interbank currency market.

Remittances moved into informal channels, import settlements stalled, and the informal curb rate surged far above official levels. Instead of calming the market, silencing price discovery and speculative liquidity deepened the currency shortage. If currency traders had been allowed to take open, view-based positions, market makers would have priced future currency scarcity into a clear forward premium.

Higher prices in official channels would have pulled export dollars home faster and kept worker remittances within regular banking routes. By continuously trading the mispricing between current scarcity and future supply, speculative market makers would have absorbed currency volatility gradually rather than leaving the system vulnerable to a sharp, sudden devaluation.

Encouraging active trading across equities, currencies, bonds, and money markets is vital for market growth. It supports new product development by ensuring the proper distribution of risk

View-based risk versus market malpractice

To regulate effectively, authorities must separate honest, view-based speculation from financial crimes. The two activities differ completely in intent, method, and market impact.

View-based speculation relies on publicly available information, macro trends, and economic analysis. Traders risk their own capital on an uncertain future. They might be right, or they might suffer heavy losses. This open risk-taking helps markets discover fair asset prices and keeps trading active.

Market abuse operates through fraud and unfair advantages. Insider trading exploits confidential, non-public data to extract guaranteed profits at the expense of ordinary investors. Price cartels, circular trading, and false accounting distort market reality to deceive the public. These criminal acts destroy market integrity and require severe regulatory penalties. Conflating informed, view-based risk with financial fraud leads to bad policy, driving legitimate capital away and leaving markets dry.

A market-based imperative

Global financial centers understand that liquidity costs money, and risk-takers provide that service. Policymakers in Bangladesh must stop treating market traders as enemies.

Encouraging active trading across equities, currencies, bonds, and money markets is vital for market growth. It supports new product development by ensuring the proper distribution of risk. This process creates a resilient financial ecosystem capable of absorbing macroeconomic shocks. That institutional capability also builds investor confidence and attracts foreign capital. Speculators do not create financial trouble; their trading provides the depth that helps the wider economy handle market stress.

* Sajed ul Islam is a senior banking executive and financial markets specialist with three decades of global institutional experience across treasury, capital markets, and corporate governance.

item.title: Warnings ignored: More than 500 websites at risk
item.description:
A new security vulnerability has been identified in PHP, putting more than 500 websites in Bangladesh at risk. These include websites operated by both government and private organisations. The government’s cyber security agency, BGD e-Gov CIRT, has issued a warning about the new vulnerability.

According to sources at the agency, more than 500 websites and apps are running older versions of PHP. Despite being warned, the operators have not updated their software. This has raised fresh concerns about the security of the country’s digital services.

PHP stands for “Hypertext Preprocessor”. It is a programming language that works in the background, or on the back end, of websites. A recent BBC report, citing cyber security firm Wiz, said PHP is used to run 70 per cent of websites worldwide.

Last week, a group of researchers from two US cyber security firms, Calif and Wiz, identified two vulnerabilities in PHP with the help of artificial intelligence (AI). On 21 October, the PHP development team released an urgent security update worldwide to fix the two serious flaws. On 23 October, the PHP authorities announced that another vulnerability had been identified.

The latest vulnerability is linked to PHP’s session management system and a specific feature used to track the progress of file uploads. Experts say attackers could exploit this weakness to execute unauthorised commands on servers.

Monitoring by CIRT’s Cyber Threat Intelligence Unit has identified more than 500 websites at risk. Most belong to private organisations. However, financial websites and government websites providing services of public importance are also exposed to the risk.

Meanwhile, CIRT issued a warning about the issue yesterday. It said a security patch for the new vulnerability had not yet been released. The affected versions and the severity of the risk had also not been determined.

In the meantime, the agency has advised the organisations concerned to temporarily disable PHP’s “session upload progress” feature, restart the necessary server services, review software configurations and monitor suspicious activity.

Over 500 websites at risk

The two serious PHP security vulnerabilities have raised concerns about cyber security worldwide. In Bangladesh, too, various websites were taken offline before being brought back online.

Monitoring by CIRT’s Cyber Threat Intelligence Unit has identified more than 500 websites at risk. Most belong to private organisations. However, financial websites and government websites providing services of public importance are also exposed to the risk.

Junaid Miazi, Chief Technology Officer of a private hosting companyMany people assume a website is secure simply because it is running. As a result, they neglect regular software updates and security fixes. Keeping security measures up to date, however, is essential.

Asked about the issue, CIRT Project Director Nazmul Haque Khandoker told Prothom Alo, “The risk will decrease if the websites are updated. However, the number of websites identified so far is concerning.”

Warnings being ignored

Several CIRT officials said government and private organisations are still using old, vulnerable versions of PHP on their websites. Even after receiving warnings, the organisations have not provided assurances that they will apply the necessary security fixes.

The officials also fear that sensitive information belonging to citizens could be stolen and that cyberattacks could occur.

Junaid Miazi, chief technology officer (CTO) of a private hosting company, told Prothom Alo that many people assume a website is secure simply because it is running. As a result, they neglect regular software updates and security fixes. Keeping security measures up to date, however, is essential.

Who is responsible for website security?

The National Cyber Security Agency and BGD e-Gov CIRT, which operates under the Bangladesh Computer Council, play roles in protecting the country’s digital infrastructure.

CIRT works to identify cyber threats and issue warnings about security vulnerabilities. However, questions remain about how effectively the authorities ensure that organisations address these weaknesses promptly after receiving warnings and properly follow security protocols.

Information technology expert Sumon Ahmed Sabir told Prothom Alo that responsibility for a website’s security rests with the organisation that operates it.

According to him, simply assigning responsibility is not enough. There must also be a system to check whether organisations are properly following security measures.

A national framework is needed to establish cyber security standards and ensure that they are being followed, he added.

item.title: Israel has voted – but the results will be messy. Here’s how its next govt will be formed
item.description:
ISRAEL-VOTE

Exit polls in Israel’s 2026 elections suggest Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition will be significantly smaller than the bloc of parties opposing him in the next Knesset (parliament). Arab parties also look likely to dramatically increase their representation.

Yet, with neither bloc likely to gain the 61 seats required for a majority, there is a long and complicated road ahead before we can say with certainty who will be Israel’s next Prime Minister.

Polls should always be treated with caution. In Israel this is especially true, for several reasons. First, too many unpredictable factors are at play in Israel’s electoral system – a nationwide proportional representation system with a high threshold (four seats) to enter the 120-seat Knesset.

Polling certain sectors, such as the ultra-Orthodox (13% of eligible voters) and Israel’s Arab citizens (18 per cent), is very difficult due to operational and trust issues.

This year, pollsters were unable to map the views of an exceptionally high 618,000 new voters and an unprecedented 650,000 reservists and diplomats who vote in “double envelopes”, which are counted only after election day.

Finally, 810,000 of Israel’s 7.3 million eligible voters live abroad, but tens of thousands of them flew in especially to cast their votes this year.

With no camp likely able to form a majority, how will Israel’s next government be formed? What are the steps, and what political deals will be needed to build a coalition?

Step 1: endorsements

Ordinarily, Israel’s presidency is a largely symbolic position. But following elections, the president is tasked with granting a party leader the authority to negotiate forming the next government.

After the official election results are handed over to the president, the “recommendation parade” begins. In 2026, President Isaac Herzog will invite representatives of all parties that passed the minimum threshold (3.25 per cent of valid votes) to his residence in Jerusalem to ask them to recommend a candidate to be the next prime minister. This could be Likud’s prime minister Netanyahu, his rival Gadi Eisenkot – former IDF chief of staff and leader of the Yashar! (translated as “straight” or “honest”) party. It could also be anyone else, or even no one. Netanyahu remains the head of the interim government, with some limitations, until a new government is formed. This could take months.

When consultations conclude, the president summons the person he judges has the best chance of forming a government, based on the combined number of Knesset seats held by the parties that recommended this candidate. At this stage, it looks like Eisenkot would get the first go at forming a government.

Other considerations the president can weigh are which candidate has received the most recommendations and who leads the biggest party (Netanyahu’s Likud is predicted to be the biggest, as at time at publication).

However, there have been cases where the head of a relatively small party received the mandate from the president and successfully formed a government. In 2021, it was Naftali Bennett who, despite winning only seven seats, became prime minister, even though Netanyahu’s Likud was the biggest party with 30 seats.

The president’s chosen candidate has 28 days, and an additional 14 days if they ask for it, to form a government. If they fail, the president repeats the process, asking parties to again recommend a candidate (same or different). If no government is formed after two such rounds and following a third 21-day-long round run by the Knesset, the country goes to the polls again.

Step 2: political negotiations

To form the government, a chosen candidate begins marathon deliberations with party representatives, aiming to form a consensus government platform. The magic number required is 61 Knesset members to join the coalition (a majority government), or fewer but with additional support from outside the coalition (a minority government).

At this stage, each party tries to maximise its “extortion” leverage to secure as much power as possible. For example, this could be in the number and importance of ministries, control over budgets, and funding for its constituents and affiliated institutions.

At the top of the list this time will be the draft bill addressing the exemption from army service of tens of thousands of ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) men.

The Eisenkot bloc unanimously agreed to ensure enlistment of those men into the Israeli Defense Force (IDF). The Haredi parties (Shas, United Torah Judaism) will demand enshrining the exemption. The Netanyahu-aligned right-wing Religious Zionist party supports drafting the ultra-Orthodox, but through negotiating with the Haredi parties rather than forcing it on them.

Traditionally, Arab parties have stayed out of government and used coalition negotiations to gain budgets – for example, for infrastructure in Arab villages or for Arab municipalities with debts (due to crime, corruption and inefficiency).

But in 2026, the Ra’am party, led by Mansour Abbas, wants to join a no-Netanyahu coalition – as it did in 2021. This is why number two on its list is a Zionist, former senior police officer Yoav Segalovitch.

However, the party faces opposition from within Eisenkot’s bloc, as Zionist parties have stated they would not sit in the coalition with Arab parties.

Israel’s Palestinian policy is a thorny issue for Eisenkot’s bloc. While Netanyahu’s right-wing party partners encourage and facilitate settlement activity and aspire to annex the West Bank, the spectrum of views on this issue is wider on the other side.

For example, the Democrats (made of Labor and left-wing Meretz), headed by Yair Golan, support talks with the Palestinians on a Palestinian state. Yisrael Beytenu’s (Israel is our home) Avigdor Liberman, and Beyahad’s (Together) Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid reject Palestinian sovereignty as unacceptable after October 7.

Above all, the 2026 Israeli election is not about Netanyahu, but about the direction the Jewish state will take in the coming years. It may take a few more weeks before the answer is known.

item.title: Gas-fed fire in Cox’s Bazar continues for second day
item.description:
A fire believed to have been triggered by underground gas escaping during deep tube-well drilling in Inani, Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar, continued to burn on Wednesday, more than 24 hours after it broke out.
Authorities have suspended electricity supply along a 15km stretch from Monkhali to Patuartek over fears that the flames could spread to power lines. The administration has also restricted public movement within a 200-metre radius of the site.
A team of experts from the Bangladesh Petroleum Exploration and Production Company (Bapex) is scheduled to investigate the source and composition of the gas and determine the cause of the fire on Wednesday morning. The team visited the site on Tuesday night.
The experts arrived in Cox’s Bazar on Tuesday evening and reached the site around 10pm. Meanwhile, four fire service units have been working to control the blaze, but the continuous flow of gas from underground has prevented them from extinguishing it.
SM Nafifun Arham, a Bapex manager (geology) and head of the geological survey team, inspected the site and offered a preliminary assessment that drilling may have reached a gas-bearing layer about 1,000 feet below the surface.
He said gas might have travelled upwards through underground fissures or geological faults before escaping through the borehole.
According to Nafifun, once a gas-bearing layer is breached, high-pressure gas can escape through cracks in the surrounding rock and continue reaching the surface for several days. He said the gas may have caught fire after coming into contact with an external ignition source, such as a spark caused by human activity or an electrical discharge.
Based on the flame’s colour and the smoke, he suspected the gas might contain relatively heavy hydrocarbons. However, its composition cannot be confirmed until samples are collected and analysed in a laboratory. The volume of any underground gas reserves also remains unknown.
Nafifun cautioned that attempts to stop the leak or contain the pressure could force the gas through other weak points underground, potentially increasing the risk. He said the immediate priority was to ensure public safety and keep people away from the site.
The gas leak began around 7:30am on Tuesday while workers were excavating the ground to install a deep tube well at the homestead of Mohammad Abdullah, near the Inani Chhoto Khal bridge in Jaliapalong union, Ukhiya. The foul-smelling gas caught fire shortly after emerging from the ground.
Saidul Islam, an official at Ukhiya Fire Service and Civil Defence station, said four units responded to the incident but could not extinguish the flames because gas continued to escape from underground.
He said limited manpower and technical equipment had made the situation difficult to manage, prompting the team to notify higher authorities. Relevant agencies, including Bapex and Petrobangla, were subsequently informed.
The blaze has caused alarm among local residents and employees of nearby hotels. Tourism entrepreneurs Jahangir Alam and Abu Syed said a fire at Tup Tup Resort in Inani’s Patuartek area about 10 days earlier had killed 11 tourists, adding to local anxiety over the latest incident. The flames can be seen from a considerable distance.
Mohammad Al-Amin, an employee at a five-star hotel adjacent to the site, said some hotel workers lived in a room next to the area where the fire broke out.
“We are living in great fear with the fire burning like this,” he said.
Ukhiya Palli Bidyut Samity has suspended electricity supply along the approximately 15km stretch from Monkhali to Patuartek because of concerns that the flames could reach power lines.
Ukhiya Upazila Nirbahi Officer Panna Akter said authorities were advising residents to maintain a safe distance from the site. Necessary measures were being taken based on the experts’ preliminary observations, and the administration had decided to cordon off the area within a 200-metre radius.
She added that local residents had told her gas exploration might have taken place in the area during the British colonial period. The administration would seek assistance from the army and other agencies if necessary.
Authorities have decided to keep the power supply suspended until the fire risk has been assessed and the area is considered safe.

item.title: Liton returns as Bangladesh opt to bat first against West Indies in 1st Test
item.description:
Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto won the toss and elected to bat first against the West Indies in the opening Test at Mirpur on Wednesday, with wicketkeeper-batter Liton Das returning to the playing XI after recovering from a hip injury.
Liton’s availability had been uncertain after he sustained a hip joint injury following Bangladesh’s one-off Test against Afghanistan in Abu Dhabi, which forced him to miss the subsequent ODI tri-series.
However, the right-hander recovered after adequate rest and resumed batting practice before taking part in wicketkeeping drills.
Shanto had expressed optimism about Liton’s fitness ahead of the match, although he was awaiting final clearance from the medical team.
“Liton worked on his fitness this morning as well. So far, he is doing well, but the physio and trainer have not yet given me a definitive report. Hopefully, we will get good news. If everything goes well, he will play, but I have not received the 100 per cent confirmation yet,” Shanto said at the pre-match press conference.
Taskin Ahmed, who returns to the Test squad after being rested for the one-off match against Afghanistan, has been left out of the playing XI for the opening Test.
Bangladesh will look to make the most of batting first as they begin their two-match ICC World Test Championship series against the West Indies at home.

item.title: Arsenal stunned by fourth-tier Fleetwood in League Cup
item.description:
Arsenal suffered one of the most humiliating defeats in their history as the Premier League champions were stunned by fourth-tier minnows Fleetwood in a League Cup penalty shoot-out on Tuesday.
Mikel Arteta's side crashed out 5-3 on penalties in an incredible fourth round upset after the tie finished 1-1 in normal time.
Arsenal's Bruno Guimaraes had his penalty saved by Jay Lynch in the shoot-out and Conor Haughey scored Fleetwood's winner.
Aaron Loupalo-Bi's first-half goal had put Fleetwood ahead before Viktor Gyokeres equalised after the interval.
Arsenal's 16-year-old rising star Max Dowman was sent off for violent conduct in the closing stages.
Arteta paid the price for prioritising Sunday's Premier League trip to Liverpool as his decision to make nine changes backfired spectacularly.
No one would have predicted Arsenal's embarrassment regardless of Arteta's selection gamble.
They had moved level on points with Premier League leaders Manchester City after a 2-0 victory over Everton on Saturday.
But instead of extending their run of 11 wins from their 13 previous games, Arsenal returned to north London red-faced after a loss that ranks among the darkest days in the club's glittering history.
Arsene Wenger's Arsenal suffered a shock League Cup loss against fourth tier Bradford on penalties in 2012.
Arteta's team were beaten by second tier Southampton in the FA Cup last season and also lost to Nottingham Forest, then in the Championship, in the same competition in 2022.
Supporters of an older vintage will recall Arsenal's 1969 League Cup final loss against third tier Swindon and their 1992 FA Cup exit at fourth tier Wrexham.
But even those painful defeats cannot compare to this remarkable result.
For once, Arsenal fans will not have fond memories of Highbury -- Fleetwood's ground shares the same name as the Gunners' ancestral home before their move to the Emirates Stadium in 2006.
Fleetwood's tiny 5,327-capacity ground -- where goals are celebrated with a burst of children' cartoon song Captain Pugwash over the tannoy -- is a far cry from the famous marble halls and dignified grandeur of Arsenal's former stadium.
Now it will be remembered forever as the site of Arsenal's most chastening loss in the Arteta era.
Fleetwood boss Matt Lawlor wept tears of joy as disbelieving fans flooded the pitch to celebrate their club's astonishing victory.
Only Myles Lewis-Skelly and Viktor Gyokeres kept their places from the Everton game, with teenagers Dowman and Marli Salmon starting, while 18-year-old winger Ceadach O'Neill made his debut.
Languishing in 18th place in League Two, Fleetwood had lost their previous two league games against Exeter and Cheltenham, yet they showed no signs of being intimidated by their illustrious visitors.
After an eight-minute delay due to an unauthorised drone flying over the stadium, Arsenal were caught cold on a windy night by the Irish Sea.
Fleetwood are nicknamed the 'Cod Army' in reference to the town's fishing industry, so it was somewhat fitting that a mistake from Salmon netted their opener in the 21st minute.
Salmon's lack of experience was brutally exposed when Loupalo-Bi muscled his way past the 17-year-old with ease, racing into the penalty area to plant a low finish past debutant keeper Illan Meslier.
Arsenal monopolised possession after that shock, but Arteta grew visibly agitated with their lack of cutting edge.
Arteta sent on Martin Odegaard at half-time and Gyokeres bagged Arsenal's equaliser five minutes later.
It was a scrappy effort that left Fleetwood feeling aggrieved as Gyokeres wrestled with his marker before poking O'Neill's ball past Lynch from close-range.
Dowman saw red in the 85th minute, dismissing for kicking out at Harrison Neal after a strong challenge from the Fleetwood midfielder.
Although it looked a harsh decision, Arteta was unimpressed with Dowman, giving him a stern word as the midfielder trudged off.
Both teams scored their first three penalties in the shoot-out, but Guimaraes was denied by Lynch and Haughey held his nerve to seal the biggest shock in League Cup history.

item.title: Starc takes six as Australia fight back in South Africa decider
item.description:
Mitchell Starc said a "reset at lunch" led to an Australian fightback after South Africa made a flying start on the first day of the third Test at Newlands on Tuesday.
Starc finished with six for 72 as South Africa were bowled out for 329 shortly before the close in a match which will decide a series between the two leading Test nations.
It was a performance which looked unlikely as South Africa raced to 140 without loss at lunch after being sent in.
Starc was one of the bowlers punished, with the tall left-arm pacer conceding 39 runs in seven overs, including four successive boundaries by Marques Ackerman, who went on to score a rapid 95.
"We probably expected more out of the wicket," said Starc. "It was quite slow, with tennis ball bounce. They came at us hard.
"We didn't have our best stuff in the first two hours but the last two sessions were right up there. It's what we expect from this group. We had a reset at lunch and just tried to change the momentum in the field."
Ackerman, playing in his second Test, took the fight to the Australian bowlers with some dazzling strokes.
The slightly-built left-hander was on 82 not out at lunch, scored off just 75 balls.
He attacked veteran off-spinner Nathan Lyon, dancing down the pitch and hitting him over the stand at midwicket for six. But he tried one shot too many after lunch and was stranded when Lyon pushed the ball wider, giving Alex Carey an easy stumping.
Ackerman, 30, said South Africa would probably have been happy if they had been offered a total of 329 before play.
But he admitted: "We probably left a few runs out there."
Ackerman, who won a place in the side through strong domestic performances and some big scores for South Africa A, including 256 against Bangladesh A in August, is not normally an opening batsman but said he was not troubled by the adjustment.
"I have quite often had to face a new ball in my career and playing against our own fast bowlers in the nets has been good preparation," he said.

item.title: Sri Lanka crush Pakistan to knock England out of tri-series final
item.description:
Sri Lanka crushed Pakistan by eight wickets on Tuesday to eliminate England from contention for the final of the ODI tri-series.
Fast bowler Dilshan Madushanka claimed a career-best 5-34 as Pakistan were bowled out for 110 after Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis elected to field after winning the toss.
Sri Lanka reached 114-2 in just 18.1 overs, securing a comfortable victory before the floodlights at Gaddafi Stadium were fully switched on for the day-night match.
Kamindu Mendis led the chase with an unbeaten 62 off 60 balls, hitting eight fours and two sixes. He survived an early chance when the wicketkeeper dropped him before he had scored and later overturned an on-field leg-before-wicket decision on review when he was batting on 44.
Mendis completed his half-century with a pull shot for six after substitute fielder Ghazi Ghori touched the boundary with his foot while taking a catch.
Sri Lanka had earlier chased down 430 against England in Rawalpindi, the second-highest successful chase in ODI history.
Pakistan had already secured a place in the final after defeating England twice, including a dramatic one-wicket victory on Sunday, and beating Sri Lanka by 37 runs in the tournament opener.
Pakistan finished the league stage with six points from three wins, while Sri Lanka have four points. Sri Lanka will face England on Thursday ahead of Saturday's final.

item.title: India race to a historic chase to seal T20I series
item.description:
India openers, Abhishek Sharma (113) and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (45), stitched together a powerplay display for the record books, piling on 118 runs in six overs as they chased down 199 runs off just 13.2 overs against New Zealand.
This marked the second-quickest chase of a 190-run target or more (with 40 deliveries remaining), second only to Estonia’s chase of 193 against Cyprus in 2024, which they completed with 42 deliveries to spare.
With New Zealand having scored 198/3 from their quota of 20 overs, India gave little room to the hosts in their response.
Abhishek was front and centre of the chase, scoring his fourth T20I hundred. His innings included a whopping 13 maximums, the most by any Indian batter in a T20I innings.
He was accompanied from the get-go by Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, who opened the innings instead of Sanju Samson, scoring a quickfire 45 runs off 19 deliveries.
The duo put together 133 runs for the opening wicket off just 43 deliveries.
“I think the key was pretty simple. It was just me and Vaibhav, just going to enjoy there for a bit, especially in the powerplay,” Abhishek said afterwards.
The groundwork for their approach was laid in the first over itself when both the left-handed batters combined to put together 26 runs for India.
“Obviously, the way he started the first over, Vaibhav, I think that was really special. And that was the plan for us, get the momentum for the team and then just keep going,” he added.
"I think Abhishek should be given credit. If you look at his batting, he scored runs in the first six overs, but it wasn't easy. The way he batted, finishing the game in the first six overs in T20, I think it takes a lot of skill," pacer Bhuvneshwar Kumar said in the post-match press conference.
While both the batters were eventually dismissed, India managed to chase down the total with relative ease, with six wickets in hand.
Earlier, Daryl Mitchell had led the charge for New Zealand, scoring an unbeaten 89 off 52 deliveries, the highest score for the batter in the shortest format of the game.
Finn Allen (40) and Bevon Jacobs (39*) also put in important contributions with the bat. However, it proved to be too little to defend with for the hosts.
After conceding nearly 100 runs in the middle phase, Bhuvneshwar credited his bowling group for the comeback in the death overs.
"I think we were all discussing it amongst ourselves. That communication is very important. Because if the person who has bowled before tells us something about the batsman doing a particular thing.
"And it's very important in the T20 format, because as you know, it's tough for bowlers. If one or two balls turn out well because of that, it can make a big difference," Bhuvneshwar said.
New Zealand captain Mitchell Santner opened up on the result, stating it was a tough pill to swallow.
“Pretty tough to stop those guys when they're going. We have seen it before, we have seen it in the IPL. Obviously, witnessed it here in New Zealand tonight,” Santner said on India’s performance with the bat.
India are now 3-0 up in the T20I series and will next play against New Zealand on Friday, 30 October in Auckland.

Second T20I: 24 October, Christchurch (India won by four wickets)
Third T20I: 27 October, Wellington (India won by six wickets)
Fourth T20I: 30 October, Auckland
Fifth T20I: 1 November, Hamilton

item.title: Shanto eyes consistency as Bangladesh target West Indies Test series win
item.description:
Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto is determined to maintain the team's recent progress in Test cricket, saying the upcoming two-match series against the West Indies is an opportunity to take another step towards their maiden World Test Championship (WTC) final.
Shanto's side will face the West Indies in the opening Test of the two-match series at Sher-e-Bangla National Cricket Stadium in Mirpur on Wednesday.
Bangladesh, currently fourth in the WTC standings, have a realistic chance of qualifying for the final, but Shanto said the team would not be distracted by the qualification equation.
He rather preferred to focus on playing good cricket in each match and session.
"I am not thinking too far ahead. We are thinking only about this Test match, or rather, this two-Test series. If we win these matches, we can automatically achieve those goals," Shanto said in a pre-match conference at Sher-e-Bangla National Cricket Stadium today.
Bangladesh need to win at least four of their remaining six Tests, while a draw could also be crucial to their qualification hopes.
Shanto, however, said the possibility of reaching the WTC final was a source of inspiration rather than pressure.
"It's inspiring, not pressure. We want to follow our process and give 100 per cent to what we can do. We don't want to do anything extra," he said.
The Bangladesh captain expressed his satisfaction with the team's preparations, particularly the early training undertaken by players who returned home after the Afghanistan series. He admitted that the West Indies had prepared extensively, including a camp in Zimbabwe, but insisted that Bangladesh had made the most of the time available to them.
"Our players have enough experience. For the last few years, we have been playing cricket series after series, and we have gradually adapted to this situation. The players have been able to prepare in their respective environments, and I am happy with the preparation," he remarked.
Shanto also stressed the importance of consistency, saying that Bangladesh had not performed well in their last two or three Tests.
"Consistency is definitely important. We haven't played better cricket as we did previously in the last two or three Tests. We have been discussing how we can improve, and there is a lot of planning in place," he said.
He is optimistic that the team could improve its performance by another 20 to 30 percent in the coming days.
Bangladesh have made encouraging progress in Test cricket in recent years, highlighted by their victory over Australia in Darwin and their improved performances in overseas conditions. However, the drawn Test against Afghanistan left Shanto disappointed, as he believed Bangladesh should have won the match.
Despite the missed opportunity, he identified several positives from the five-day contest, particularly the players' determination to fight until the final session.
"We should have won that match, 100 per cent. But the positive thing was that we fought hard for five days, and everyone showed tremendous commitment, especially in bowling and fielding in such hot conditions," he said.
Shanto believes the experience will help Bangladesh handle similar situations more effectively in the future. Shanto also said Bangladesh had experienced options in the middle order, which provided reassurance to the captain.
He said the pace bowlers were prepared to play whenever required, depending on the conditions.
Regarding Litton Das's fitness, Shanto said the batter had completed batting and fielding practice but the team was still waiting for the final assessment from the physiotherapist and trainer.
"If everything goes well, he will play, but I have not yet received the final report," he said.

item.title: When the state turns humiliation into public spectacle
item.description:
A person can be presumed innocent in a courtroom and condemned by thousands on a smartphone screen before the first hearing begins.
In Bangladesh, videos of police raids increasingly expose detained women, men, and even children to public scrutiny, often revealing their faces and personal circumstances before the allegations against them have been established.
What makes this practice particularly troubling is not merely the invasion of privacy, but the transformation of state authority into a source of public humiliation.
When law enforcement agencies facilitate such exposure and media outlets reproduce it without sufficient scrutiny, the distinction between investigating a crime and staging a spectacle begins to disappear.
The recent incident in Purbachal, where 85 people were detained during a raid and reportedly pressured to uncover their faces before cameras, illustrates the problem.
Similar footage from establishments in Gulshan and Uttara has circulated online, inviting audiences to speculate about the identities, occupations, and private lives of those detained.
Yet the central question is not whether the public should know about suspected wrongdoing. It is whether exposing the faces and personal circumstances of people who have not been convicted contributes anything meaningful to public understanding of the alleged offense.
This question matters because public humiliation is not an incidental consequence of these videos. It has become part of their appeal.
A raid offers the drama of sudden discovery, a group of detainees supplies the visual material, and a camera turns the encounter into content.
The audience is invited to feel that it has witnessed wrongdoing being punished, even when no court has determined that an offense occurred.
In this arrangement, suspicion becomes a form of guilt, exposure becomes a substitute for accountability, and humiliation acquires the appearance of justice.
The underlying danger is that punishment begins to precede the judicial process. A criminal investigation is supposed to establish facts, test evidence, and identify responsibility through lawful procedures. Publicly displaying detainees, by contrast, can impose a social penalty before those procedures have run their course.
A person may eventually be released, acquitted, or found to have had no involvement in the alleged offense, but the digital record remains. Images can be copied, reposted, downloaded, and detached from their original context. A subsequent correction rarely travels as far as the original accusation.
For women, the consequences can be particularly severe. Exposure may invite moral judgment, harassment, and reputational damage that extend to their families and professional lives.
In a society where women's conduct is frequently subjected to disproportionate scrutiny, the publication of footage from a police raid can function as an instrument of social punishment, regardless of the legal merits of the case.
Their identities become the story, while the evidence, the circumstances of the raid, and the conduct of the authorities receive comparatively less attention.
The result is a disturbing inversion of accountability: The people whose alleged conduct requires investigation become publicly identifiable, while the decisions of those exercising state power may remain largely unexamined.
Men are not immune to this practice. Videos of searches, phone inspections, and interrogations can expose private communications, personal associations, and intimate details to strangers.
Children face an even more alarming risk. The circulation of a schoolgirl's video following allegations about her private life demonstrates how quickly a moment of vulnerability can become a permanent public record.
Bangladesh's Children Act restricts the publication of information that may identify a child in circumstances covered by its provisions. Yet the existence of a legal prohibition does not automatically protect children when digital audiences reward exposure and those responsible for sharing the footage fail to consider its consequences.
The Constitution of Bangladesh provides important protections relevant to this debate. Article 31 concerns protection of the law and treatment in accordance with law, while Article 35 includes safeguards against compelled self-incrimination and torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights also recognizes the presumption of innocence and protection against arbitrary interference with privacy, family, home, and reputation.
These principles are not suspended because someone has been detained or because a video attracts considerable attention. Nor does the public's curiosity automatically establish a public interest in revealing a person's identity.
The distinction between public interest and public curiosity deserves particular emphasis. Reporting that authorities have conducted a raid, detained individuals, or uncovered evidence of suspected wrongdoing may serve a legitimate public purpose.
Yet, identifying the people involved, broadcasting their faces, or displaying their distress requires a separate justification. Their identities may be relevant in some cases, particularly when authorities are seeking public assistance or when identification is necessary to understand a matter of genuine public importance.
But such exceptions should not become routine practice. The question should always be whether disclosure is necessary, proportionate, and supported by a clear public interest, rather than whether it is likely to generate attention.
This is where the conduct of media organizations becomes inseparable from the problem. Journalism cannot surrender its editorial judgment merely because footage comes from an official source.
Police briefings, photographs, and videos are not neutral windows into reality; they reflect decisions about what to record, what to disclose, and how an operation should be presented.
When journalists publish such material without asking why detainees are being exposed, whether the footage is necessary, or whether its circulation could cause disproportionate harm, they risk becoming distributors of an official narrative rather than independent observers of state power.
The economic and technological incentives of digital journalism make this failure easier to understand, though not to excuse.
Faces, confrontation, and apparent scandal attract clicks and shares. A video that invites moral condemnation may travel faster than a carefully reported account of investigative procedure or legal safeguards.
As mobile journalism and live broadcasting expand, the cost of recording and distributing an encounter has fallen dramatically.
Editorial restraint, however, has not necessarily advanced at the same pace. The result is an environment in which the capacity to expose people has grown faster than the willingness to consider whether they should be exposed.
There is also a serious institutional question for law enforcement. If journalists are informed about raids in advance, accompany officers, and receive footage from official sources, clear rules are needed to establish the limits of access and disclosure.
Recording material for evidentiary purposes is not equivalent to distributing it for publicity. A video may have legitimate investigative value while being entirely unsuitable for public release.
The authority to investigate suspected crime should not be treated as an unrestricted licence to display the people under investigation. If allegations of threats to expose detainees are substantiated, they demand especially serious scrutiny because the prospect of public disgrace could become a means of coercion or extortion.
Bangladesh's courts have previously raised concerns about presenting arrested persons and suspects before the media, including judicial interventions in 2012 and 2015 and observations concerning media briefings during ongoing investigations in 2019.
The persistence of similar practices suggests that judicial concern alone cannot establish an effective culture of restraint.
Clear operational rules, enforceable accountability, and consistent editorial standards are needed to translate legal principles into everyday practice.
Any policy should distinguish legitimate public disclosure from unnecessary identification, protect children and vulnerable people, and establish consequences for unauthorized or coercive dissemination of footage.
Ultimately, the issue is larger than the privacy of individual detainees. It concerns the kind of relationship citizens are permitted to have with the institutions that exercise power over them.
When an arrest becomes an opportunity for public shaming, the state communicates that dignity is conditional and that suspicion can strip a person of ordinary protections.
When media organizations amplify that message, they help normalize a culture in which exposure is mistaken for evidence and humiliation for justice.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.title: Can Bangladesh’s cyber police outrun its institutions?
item.description:
A police officer watching a crowded street sees only what is in front of them. A cyber police officer can potentially see patterns across thousands of phones, accounts, images, and videos.
Bangladesh is now developing the capacity to do much more of that.
On October 1, the country launched its new Cyber Police Unit with an approved structure of 4,592 posts. The unit is tasked with investigating cyber and financial crimes, analyzing digital evidence, monitoring social media and the dark web, and using AI-assisted video analytics and facial identification. Cyber desks are planned for police stations, alongside a 24/7 cyber support centre.
The case for expanding cyber policing is straightforward. Criminal activity increasingly leaves a digital trail, and police need the expertise and technology to follow it.
But a more capable cyber police force also raises a less comfortable question: Can the institutions governing these new powers develop as quickly as the powers themselves?
Digital policing is not merely about catching criminals more efficiently. It also concerns who can access information, how it is interpreted, and what happens when the state gets it wrong.
Bangladesh is not starting from scratch. The Criminal Investigation Department (CID) has operated its Cyber Police Centre since 2017 to deal with cybercrime and related digital investigations.
Since 2020, the Bangladesh Police’s Police Cyber Support for Women (PCSW) has provided legal and technological assistance to women facing cybercrime, including counselling and referrals to police stations, specialised units and victim-support centres. Broader reporting channels include police stations and the national emergency service, 999.
The challenge is not just creating more places for victims to report. It is making these channels work together.
A woman reporting image-based abuse, for example, should not have to know whether her case belongs with a local police station, a new cyber desk, the Cyber Police Centre, PCSW, or another specialized unit.
Her case should reach the right expertise without requiring her to navigate the bureaucracy herself.
That becomes more important as the new unit expands. The 4,592 figure represents approved posts, not a fully staffed force. Existing police personnel will initially fill positions before additional recruitment. The cyber desks and 24/7 support centre will also have to move from organisational plans to functioning services.
But the harder questions begin once the police have the data.
Who can access sensitive digital evidence? How long should it be retained? When can it be shared with another agency? How should investigators document the use of AI-assisted systems? And what happens when an automated identification or analysis is wrong?
A mistaken police conclusion about a digital identity, image, or online interaction can affect an investigation, a person’s reputation, or their freedom. As analytical tools become more powerful, scrutiny of their conclusions becomes more important.
Bangladesh’s Personal Data Protection Act 2026 establishes a broader framework for protecting personal data while allowing processing without consent where necessary for the prevention, detection, inquiry, investigation or prosecution of offences.
That is important for law enforcement. But a general data-protection framework cannot by itself determine how every police database, forensic system or AI-assisted tool should be operated.
Accountability matters especially because Bangladesh’s recent police oversight framework remains unsettled.
The 2025 Police Commission Ordinance included a mechanism for citizen complaints, but that framework is no longer in effect.
This creates a sequencing problem. It is relatively easy to acquire technology and create new police posts. It is harder to build durable institutions capable of scrutinizing how that technology is used.
Once databases, analytical systems, and specialized investigative practices become embedded, changing the rules around them becomes more difficult.
Bangladesh should build safeguards alongside capability. The new Cyber Police Unit should connect with existing victim-support and referral services rather than set up another isolated reporting channel.
Police should have clear operational rules governing access to, retention, and sharing of digital evidence, as well as procedures for documenting and challenging consequential errors in automated analysis. Citizens also need credible avenues to question misuse of digital investigative powers.
The future of cyber policing will not be determined only by what police can see. It will be determined by what they are allowed to do with what they see, and whether citizens have meaningful ways to challenge them when they get it wrong.
Ashfaq Ferdous is an academic at Southeast University, Bangladesh, and a former Assistant Superintendent of Police with Bangladesh Police.
